title: Agony and ecstasy for Australian duo in WNBA Finals game seven
text:
Opal Miela Sowah has etched her name in Australian women's basketball history books as her Golden State Valkyries overcame Izzy Borlase's Atlanta Dream 68-63 to win the WNBA championship.

The 26-year-old entered the league's first-ever game seven at San Francisco's Chase Centre on Saturday (Sunday AEDT) looking to join the 11 previous Australian winners of the top women's basketball competition in the world.

That list includes some of the country's biggest basketball names such as Lauren Jackson and Penny Taylor, while Sowah was also aiming to become the first Australian winner since Cayla George in 2023.

The Opal didn't take the court as she is on a player development contract, making her ineligible to feature in the playoffs.

But Sowah was an avid supporter from the sidelines, as she helped spur on Gabby Williams to a masterclass as the forward posted 30 points and four blocks.

Of those, 28 were in the second half — a WNBA finals record for most points by a player in a half.

Izzy Borlase had some big moments as her Dream went down in game seven. (Getty Images: Matthew Huang)

Ex-Bendigo Spirit star Veronica Burton was also busy, registering 10 points, 11 rebounds and five assists to help Golden State claim a maiden championship in the franchise's second season.

While Sowah will bask in title glory, her Opals teammate Borlase will not after her team missed a golden opportunity to claim a historic first championship.

The 22-year-old played another important role off the bench as she recorded eight points and two rebounds in 14 minutes of game time.

Her best moment came in the third quarter when she coolly sank a three to end the Valkyries' 6-0 run before she later drove to the basket and earned a three-point play in the fourth period.

A title would have capped off a remarkable year for Borlase, who became the WNBL's youngest MVP in 15 years, made her Women's World Cup debut with the Opals and played her first minutes in the American league.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

title: Suspended Powerhouse CEO denies wrongdoing as 14 disclosures revealed
text:
The curtain is about to be raised on Sydney's so-called 'Opera House of the west' with the new Powerhouse Parramatta due to the open on November 7.

But the $915 million project remains under a cloud with a Minns government investigation into alleged misconduct by unnamed executives, a whistleblower report, and a referral of undisclosed allegations to the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC).

While supporters of the suspended CEO, Lisa Havilah, have launched a petition for her immediate reinstatement, questions persist over how millions of dollars in public money has been managed.

On the eve of the grand opening, Ms Havilah is fighting back against the government, saying that she acted with integrity.

7.30 can reveal Ms Havilah made 14 declarations of perceived conflicts of interest and matters that may give rise to a conflict of interest during her tenure, according to internal documents released under state freedom of information laws.

The declarations, since 2019, include entries about former work associates of Ms Havilah's hired to consult for the Powerhouse, and a $1.9 million marketing contract awarded to a company founded by former Powerhouse trustee, Mark Hassell.

In all 14 cases, there were "actions proposed to mitigate the real or perceived conflict", according to the documents.

Ms Havilah was suspended in August amid a governance and procurement investigation.

The Powerhouse Parramatta is due to open on November 7. (Supplied: Powerhouse Parramatta)

Ms Havilah is not authorised to speak publicly but her spokesperson told 7.30 in a statement that the records show she acted properly.

"No findings have been made against Ms Havilah, who denies any wrongdoing and at all times has maintained the highest standards of integrity," the statement said.

"The disclosures in question were made out of an abundance of caution to ensure transparency regarding her legitimate professional relationships. The disclosures were made for the purpose of perceived conflicts of interest and did not give rise to any actual conflict of interest."

Declarations of conflicts of interest, real or perceived, are widely used by public institutions to ensure integrity of processes, particularly in the awarding of public contracts.

The Museum's own declaration form states that: "Conflicts of interest are not wrong in themselves. It is how they are managed that is important."

Ms Havilah's spokesperson said that none of the disclosures resulted in any personal gain for her.

It took four years for the Powerhouse Parramatta to be built. (Supplied: Powerhouse Museum)

Millions of dollars in contracts

In 2019, Ms Havilah declared "a perceived conflict of interest" over the hiring of three former work associates as consultants for the Powerhouse Museum, Lisa Ffrench, Amanda Burgess and Cass O'Connor.

The documents state that "the perceived conflict has been disclosed, and the procurement was undertaken by the Executive Officer, who has noted this conflict. The contract will also be managed by the Executive Officer".

7.30 understands the Executive Officer referred to was not Ms Havilah.

Prior to becoming Powerhouse CEO in 2018, Ms Havilah was director of arts and performance venue, Carriageworks in Sydney's Eveleigh.

Some of her previous links to Carriageworks were declared in the documents.

An entry in May 2021 declared that during her time at Carriageworks, "Felix Media were a resident company".

Lisa Havilah was the CEO of Carriageworks from 2011 until 2018. (Supplied: Museum of Arts and Applied Sciences)

Felix Media was awarded a $2.5 million contract (before rebates) over two other applicants to deliver a documentary film about the setting up of Powerhouse Parramatta.

In January this year, Ms Havilah noted "I have two conflicts to declare" as she had previously worked with public relations companies Articulate PR and Original Spin.

The documents reveal a "perceived conflict of interest" was identified in November 2025 over a $1.9m marketing contract awarded to a "creativity-driven investment company" called Ki Community, founded by former Powerhouse trustee, Mark Hassell.

The 12-month contract was part of a selective request for tender and was to deliver an "integrated marketing, communications, and engagement plan" for Powerhouse Parramatta.

"The perceived risk relates to potential public or stakeholder perception of preferential treatment or informational advantage", the documents state.

This risk was mitigated "to ensure transparency and fairness".

"With these measures, the residual risk is assessed as low-moderate, noting that transparency and equal access to information substantially mitigate the risk of any actual advantage," the document said.

"All respondents received equal access to the scoping information."

The Powerhouse Parramatta project is being investigated over alleged misconduct and has been referred to the ICAC. (ABC News: Anton Rose, Monish Nand)

In July, the Museum's Chief Operating Officer, Mark Wilsdon, also stepped aside.

In a disclosure of conflict of interest form signed by him in May 2025, he wrote "I have work (sic) with Mark in my capacity as COO through FARM (Finance Audit and Risk Management Committee) and (Powerhouse) Trust".

"This perceived conflict will be managed through the procurement process. Other senior Powerhouse staff will also be involved. Mark Hassell will not be part of the team working with Powerhouse on this engagement. This perceived conflict will be appropriately mitigated by these actions."

A separate letter from Ki Community in November 2025 released to 7.30 declares that "Mark Hassell has not participated in, contributed to, or provided any input — directly or indirectly — into the preparation or submission of our tender response".

"He has not been involved in any way regarding the strategy, pricing, technical content, or supporting documentation for this tender."

7.30 contacted Ki Community but did not receive a reply.

Alleged misconduct probe continues

The Minns government had concerns about Powerhouse management as far back as March 2025 when Arts Minister John Graham asked his department to launch a fact-finding assessment.

A referral to the ICAC was also made at the time. The ICAC would not tell 7.30 whether the referral was still active.

The $915 million Powerhouse Parramatta project has been referred to ICAC. (ABC News)

7.30 requested the report of the government's assessment under freedom of information laws but was refused access because of secrecy provisions under the ICAC Act.

In December 2025, Mr Graham escalated the matter to a formal misconduct investigation.

By mid-2026, "a range of allegations were put to a number of Powerhouse executives," Mr Graham told a state parliamentary committee in August.

In response to the release of the disclosure documents, Mr Graham told 7.30:

"After seven years of hard work, from hundreds of people, the government and team at the Powerhouse Parramatta are focused on making sure when the doors swing open next week, everyone can enjoy a truly great museum experience.

"All public servants, including senior executives, have an obligation to declare and manage any actual, potential, or perceived conflicts of interests appropriately.

"An investigation into allegations relating to procurement and governance practices at the Powerhouse is progressing. It is not appropriate to comment on matters that are under investigation."

The Powerhouse declined to comment.

title: Return of V8 Superboats a roaring success, says organiser
text:
A "big risk" for a rural town has paid off, resulting in a sell-out crowd for the return of V8 Superboat racing in Victoria.

The Elmore Events Centre, 50km north-east of Bendigo, has welcomed jet boat racing back to Victoria about 15 years after the closure of the sport's track in Melton, west of Melbourne.

The town of Elmore, population 850, made its debut on the V8 Superboats Championship scene on Saturday, hosting round one of the 2026-27 season.

Elmore's first V8 Superboats event was sold out. (Supplied: V8 Superboats)

"Once the rain cleared, it turned into a tremendous day," said Elmore Events Centre executive manager Derek Shotton.

" We got maximum crowd, good results and good racing. "

Jet boats are a new addition for the not-for-profit venue, which is better known for hosting agricultural field days, equestrian events, scouts and tractor pull competitions.

Derek Shotton says the track was designed to be technically challenging for drivers. (ABC Rural: Warwick Long)

Mr Shotton said jet boat racing would help ensure the venue's future sustainability.

"It was a big risk for us to go into developing this, and it was quite gratifying to see both the competitors and patrons so embracing and positive about it all," he said.

Racing returned to Victoria on Saturday at Elmore. (Supplied: V8 Superboats)

They broke ground on the 1km-long, 3m-wide and 750mm-deep course less than a year ago.

On Saturday, the track's design challenged drivers' technical skills, rather than maximum speeds.

"There were plenty of mishaps and mis-corners and boats landing on islands, that adds to the excitement," Mr Shotton said.

Disturbed Racing Team took out the LS class on Saturday. (Supplied: V8 Superboats)

Victoria's return to national stage

Driver Jade Atchison and her navigator Erin Kearney, from the Disturbed Racing Team based on the NSW Central Coast, won the LS class event.

They said they relished the technical challenge of Elmore's new track.

"It was a bit of a go-kart track which I've kind of always preferred," Ms Atchison said.

"It's fun, it's a bit different. The longer tracks, you're worrying more about speed," Ms Atchison said.

The Elmore jet boat track is designed to technically challenge drivers. (Supplied: V8 Superboats)

She said V8 Superboat's return to Victoria was a positive for the sport.

"There was such a good turnout on the weekend, I think everyone's really impressed with it and happy it's gone ahead," she said.

"The more tracks, the better; everyone who's in the sport is really passionate about it and just wants to see it flourish."

Mr Shotton also said the sport's return "shouldn't be underrated".

"Finding the right piece of ground where you're not close to residential areas, and you can do this sort of racing has been a hard try," he said.

" For us to be able to do this puts Victoria back on the national stage. "

Elmore will host two rounds per season for the next five years.

Organisers said they are already looking at improvements before the next race, including installing a third viewing bank for spectators.

The next event in Elmore will be held on March 13, with a tractor pull and lawnmower racing to be held on the same day.

title: Fremantle's $596m bridge opens four months ahead of schedule
text:
Thousands of people are expected to walk across the new Fremantle traffic bridge today after it opened to the public months ahead of schedule.

The new 500-metre bridge, named the Walyalup Bridge, marks the next chapter for the port city's historic Swan River crossing and came with a price tag of $596 million — more than double the original estimate.

The structure is the first "extra-dosed" bridge to be built in Australia, combining both cantilevers and cable stay supports.

The opening of the bridge was a lively, colourful affair, with bands and musicians entertaining the crowd. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch )

Gladys Arundel was among the first to cross the bridge, 87 years after attending the opening of the old bridge in 1939 as a fourteen year old.

"We were in high school just down the road and they decided we would all walk down here for the opening … it was very exciting," she said.

" I am very thrilled to be repeating history. "

Gladys Arundel says she first crossed the bridge as a 14 year old. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch )

Jan Middleton, who survived a dramatic 10-metre plunge off the old bridge in her car 70 years ago, was also among the huge crowd.

Jan Middleton (right) speaks with Rita Saffioti. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch )

Feat of engineering

The previous 86-year-old heritage-listed bridge was closed in February and progressively dismantled as the new bridge was built around it.

The Fremantle Traffic Bridge pictured while under construction. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

The new bridge has the same number of traffic lanes but wider pedestrian paths and a higher clearance for boats.

Construction was expected to take 12 months but has been completed about four months ahead of schedule.

The new bridge is a joint state and federal government project, with a price tag of $596 million. (Supplied: WA government)

Transport Minister Rita Saffioti thanked everyone involved in the project, as well as the community and local businesses for their patience.

"We managed to move people throughout this area with some delays but not anywhere near what people were expecting," she said.

"This is an iconic project that — as we drive past for decades to come — people will look and say 'what a beautiful bridge.'"

Federal member for Fremantle Josh Wilson, Rita Saffioti (centre) and state member for Fremantle Simone McGurk cut the ribbon. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch )

She attributed the cost blowout of the project primarily to the redesign of the bridge.

"We attempted a number of solutions … the version before the final version had a complete reconfiguration of all the roads, that would have disrupted traffic for years," Ms Saffioti said.

"We came up with a method that disrupted the community the least, that delivered the best outcome.”

The bridge construction was initially expected to take a year. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch )

Steeped in history

Walyalup Bridge is the fifth iteration of the Fremantle traffic bridge. The first was built by convicts in the mid-1800s and the most recent to be replaced was opened in 1939, with a 40 year design life.

Ms Saffioti said much consideration was given to preserving its history.

“There has been some wood that’s been preserved including the timber decking ... and some of the pylons have been incorporated into the artwork," she said.

The first Fremantle traffic bridge, pictured in 1905, with North Fremantle in the background. (Supplied: State Library Western Australia)

When the bridge closed in February, there had been significant concerns traffic congestion would be intense across the one remaining crossing, the Stirling Bridge.

The government changed traffic signals, turning lanes and put in other measures to ease traffic flow, and in the end the congestion was not as bad as feared.

There were also changes to the local transport network to accommodate the closure, including additional train and bus services, more free parking bays for SmartRider users and increased monitoring of traffic via CCTV.

It is hoped local business will benefit from the huge crowds attending the opening. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch )

Local business on both sides of the river had also warned of potentially severe economic impacts.

Some have since closed and others reported a drop in customers, while others said the closure was not as bad as they feared.

Fremantle Traffic Bridge closing date revealed The WA government could consider limiting truck movements across the Stirling Bridge at peak hour to limit traffic congestion when the Fremantle Traffic Bridge closes, the deputy premier says.

The Cyclists' Action Group has condemned the new bridge as "the most unsafe design for pedestrians, cyclists and mothers with prams built over the rivers near Perth since at least 1980".

"The major design flaw is the lack of a grade-separated crossing under the north end of the bridge for vulnerable road users to cross Queen Victoria Street safely," the group said in a statement.

title: Government will not promise net savings in budget update, despite inflation pressure
text:
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher says growing pressures on the federal budget mean the government cannot promise it will find overall savings in its December update, even as Australians brace for another interest rate rise amid ongoing high inflation.

On Wednesday Treasurer Jim Chalmers also refused to commit to net savings in the mid-year budget update following a worse-than-expected inflation figure of 4.3 per cent over the year to September, which lifted expectations of another rate hike when the Reserve Bank meets on Tuesday.

The finance minister told ABC Insiders despite pressure being put on the government to rein in its spending, she would not pre-commit to overall savings.

"I can't, I don't want to pre-empt the [Expenditure Review Committee] process. We will go through that ... but there is enormous effort being placed, particularly by Jim and myself on the savings side," Senator Gallgher said.

"We are doing a lot of work on the savings side but I can’t get ahead of decisions that haven’t been made yet."

The minister rejected suggestions the pressure to find savings was causing tension inside cabinet, saying it was healthy for ministers to have "robust" debate and bring different perspectives.

Senator Gallagher added that the government's record in each of its previous budgets and mid-year updates had been to deliver overall improvements to the budget, and that in recent budgets its policy decisions had also found more savings than new spending.

The Reserve Bank's chief economist said last week that government spending remained a contributor to ongoing inflation, even if the government points to the war in Iran as the "primary driver".

Treasurer downplays further fuel discounts Faced with another high inflation result and the likelihood of a rate hike next Tuesday, Treasurer Jim Chalmers calls for "perspective" and points to external factors.

The treasurer has previously warned that the cost of borrowing would add billions of dollars in additional costs to the budget, as long-term expectations that global interest rates would remain higher for longer were priced into bonds.

Senator Gallagher said other pressures on the budget were also growing, including in health and aged care.

She said the government's spending measures in those pressure areas were necessary to rescue a Medicare system "in freefall" and clear processing backlogs for veterans.

"If you go back to … the Howard era, you know, they were not dealing with AUKUS, they were not dealing with aged care," Senator Gallagher said.

"They weren't dealing with Medicare falling over there, all of these pressures that are coming. So there has to be some acknowledgement of that. We are living in a different world."

The government maintains that the budget is helping to tackle inflation.

However ahead of his departure to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese acknowledged that the Reserve Bank only had a single "blunt instrument" in the inflation fight.

The remaining levers to reduce demand in the economy rest with federal and state governments.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor told radio station 2GB that the government could do more to avert further rate rises.

"The government can commit tomorrow to take pressure off interest rates and inflation, that would send a strong signal to the Reserve Bank [that] they don't need to raise," Mr Taylor said.

"But they won't do it."

The Reserve Bank's chief economist Sarah Hunter said last week that state and federal government spending was "definitely" contributing to demand pressures in the economy, before adding that it was not the RBA's place to advice government on its spending.

Frontbench minister Murray Watt told News24 demand growth in the economy tripled in the private sector last financial year, while government demand growth halved.

"The substantial portion of the growth in spending in the economy is happening in the private sector rather than in the public sector. Now, I'm not being critical of people who are spending money, going to restaurants, buying a car, whatever it is that they're they're spending money on. But that's where most of the spending [growth] is happening," Senator Watt said.

"And that, of course, is contributing to inflation, as is fuel prices."

title: Shark sightings force Noosa Triathlon to scrap swim leg
text:
Organisers of the Noosa Triathlon in Queensland were forced to cancel the swim leg of the famous event at the last minute after shark sightings just an hour before the race began.

The Noosa event is the largest Olympic distance triathlon in the world and draws 8,500 athletes and 20,000 spectators each year.

Noosa Main Beach was temporarily closed on Saturday after sharks were spotted offshore.

On Saturday night, organisers modified the event to reduce the swimming distance to about 1 kilometre in order to keep swimmers in the shallows.

But early on Sunday morning, plans were thrown into chaos after organisers scrapped the swim leg entirely only an hour before the race started.

Noosa Heads surf lifesavers,who were due to monitor the event on jet skis and boards, refused to enter the water after another sighting at first light.

Matt Hauser celebrates winning the elite category of the 2026 Noosa Triathlon. (Supplied: Korupt Vision)

Head of operations Rebecca Van Pooss said it was a tough decision.

"We knew that it was a potential this morning, so we had a contingency plan ready to go because of that," she said.

"In the circumstances we had this morning, [lifesavers] wouldn't put those people out on the water, which is totally understandable.

"So, based on that decision, we made our decision that we also can't put athletes in the water."

Timing was tight, with shark surveillance beginning at first light ahead of a 6:15am start.

The decision to modify the event did not leave much time for athletes to recalibrate their race plans.

"Surf lifesaving's protocol is no-one entering the water for 60 minutes after the last sighting," Ms Van Pooss said.

"So, for us, an hour out from race start, we decided to make the call then because we didn't really have the additional time to push our starts any later."

Ms Van Pooss said the cancellation was unprecedented in the event's 43-year history.

"This is the first one that we've had to cancel in its entirety, but it's not unusual to have to make some sort of contingency decisions around course design and distance," she said.

Natalie Van Coevorden won the elite women's category in a time of 1:58:11. (Supplied: Korupt Vision)

Surf Lifesaving Queensland safety manager Matt Thompson acknowledged the decision was disappointing.

"The best outcome is always preventing an incident before it happens, and the ability to identify potential threats early and act quickly is critical to keeping Queenslanders safe in the water," he said.

The event, which became a duathlon, was won by Matt Hauser, who backed up his victory last year.

He completed the race in 1:39:34 after organisers added a 5km run in place of the swim.

The fastest female athlete was Natalie Van Coevorden, who won a thrilling race, crossing the line just 15 seconds ahead of second-placed Richelle Hill.

Competitors then cycled 40km and ran 10km for the other legs.

title: SA's historic Gladstone Gaol reopens with ghost tours
text:
Following a period of closure, one of regional South Australia’s historic landmarks has reopened its doors to the public, with new caretakers leaning into the site’s dark heritage.

This year Lantern Ghost Tours licensed the Gladstone Gaol site from the Department of Environment and Water.

This weekend, just in time for Halloween, the company opened the doors to the public for the first time, with sold-out ghost tours welcoming thrill-seekers and history enthusiasts alike to the now 145-year-old facility.

Naomi Bailey, the project coordinator for Gladstone Gaol, said it was exciting to have people back.

"The community really wanted to be here as well, they were showing it through booking of the tours, and the takeaway was the interest. We sold out," Ms Bailey said.

Lantern Ghost Tours' Naomi Bailey is the project coordinator for the recently reopened Gladstone Gaol. (ABC News: Clem Stanley)

"We had to open additional tours, and we've got really strong bookings every Saturday night."

Local tourism asset

Locals also shared Ms Bailey’s excitement to have the Gladstone Gaol’s gates open once again.

The Gladstone Gaol in 1929. (Supplied: State Library of South Australia)

Gladstone Community Development and Tourism Association president David Catford said it was a surprise when the previous operators retired in 2022.

"I think that the community has come to realise what it means not having it open," Mr Catford said.

" I have described it as the 'jewel in the crown' of the Southern Flinders tourism area because really, it's a unique site and it's an important part of getting people to come here and be tourists and see and enjoy our region. "

Mr Catford said it was a surprise when the previous operators retired in 2022. (ABC News: Arj Ganesan)

A once-off open day in 2025 was attended by some 1,300 people, which Mr Catford said proved interest in the prison was still there.

Dark history to bright future

Sitting on the cusp of the Southern Flinders Ranges and Mid-North regions, authorities in 1879 at the time determined that Gladstone would become home to a new prison, aimed at taking pressure off jails at Port Augusta and in Adelaide.

The jail operated in its intended capacity for just shy of 100 years.

Opening in 1881, its prisoner intake varied over the years, going from an all-gender prison to male-only, to a military prison during World War II, and later took on a focus more to reintegrate inmates back to society.

The jail has reopened to the public after a four-year closure. (ABC News: Arj Ganesan)

By 1975 – and still not having plumbing in the building – the government of the day closed the facility.

Gladstone local and tour guide Steve Schultz said the community acted quickly at the time to preserve the site and its history.

"It's been a long battle ever since then to keep it open and at least have it accessible to the public basically," he said.

In the years since, the jail's uses have varied, from previous ghost tour iterations, to hosting accommodation and events.

Citing a downturn in volunteers after the COVID-19 pandemic, the previous caretakers hung up the keys in 2022.

A spooky reopening

Lindi and Shelley made the trip from Clare on Friday night, with the hope of experiencing something paranormal.

Both having fond memories of visits to the jail in its time as accommodation and an events venue, Lindi said its return to the community was "awesome".

"I think this is fantastic," she said.

Lindi and Shelley were glad to visit the tourist destination again. (ABC News: Arj Ganesan)

Ms Bailey said the company planned to launch a café on the site, and restoration works that would allow for events and visitors’ further exploration of the site’s history.

"We really want to balance the heritage nature of the site and really complement it with events and activities that are coming through," she said.

Anthony Van Zeventer was passing by en route to Darwin and was happy to see the site active again. (ABC News: Arj Ganesan)

Among the visitors on Friday was Anthony Van Zeventer, who stopped by while travelling from Philip Island to Darwin, without realising it was opening night.

"I think it's great that the community's got behind it and that they're reopening it again," Mr Van Zeventer said.

title: Should every Australian worker get paid reproductive leave?
text:
When Georgia miscarried her first pregnancy, she felt she couldn't take as much leave as she needed.

The graphic designer, in her 20s, experienced pregnancy loss at 13 weeks earlier this year, saying it was "emotionally super traumatic", but she returned to work almost immediately.

"Emotionally and physically it was one of the most painful things I've ever been through and I only took two days off.

"There's sort of no guidelines or there was nothing written into any of our policies about miscarriage and what you do and what's expected of you."

Loading...

While that experience stood out, Georgia said "hormones flying'' and physical discomfort linked to her menstrual cycle was something she faced regularly, but taking time off work didn't feel like an option.

"If I was to have a day off because of period pain, I think I would actually make something else up and just say I have stomach pain," Georgia said.

"It still feels like I have to cover it. I still feel there's guilt and a stigma around using period pain as an excuse."

A federal inquiry is considering whether Australia's National Employment Standards (NES) are still fit for purpose, with several submissions pitching a need for reproductive leave, among other suggestions. The inquiry's recommendations are expected later this year.

Some unions, lawyers and advocates are pushing for at least 10 days of non-cumulative paid reproductive leave on top of existing sick leave.

So, what could the leave cover?

Queensland public sector workers are entitled to 10 days of paid reproductive health leave. (Pexels: Sora Shimazaki)

Some submissions to the inquiry suggest reproductive leave could cover things such as fertility treatment, miscarriage, menstrual pain, menopause and endometriosis.

Some suggest reproductive leave could cover men too, for things such as prostate cancer screening, vasectomies and other allied health conditions.

Advocates call for it to be in addition to the standard 10 days of sick leave, not instead of it.

And they say it's not just about leave, it's also about workplaces offering more flexibility.

Georgia believes reproductive leave would be significantly helpful.

"Ideally I would be able to work from home but like have my heat pack, wear elastic waist pants, and move around so that I'm lying on the floor or squatting or sitting cross-legged or moving around so my belly feels more comfortable."

She believes many workplaces weren't designed with women's health in mind.

"Working traditionally was for men. It was built around men. There was no consideration of the female cycle."

Reproductive leave overseas

Several countries have introduced policies recognising the impact of menstrual health at work.

Spain became the first European country to introduce paid menstrual leave in 2023.

Japan has had menstrual leave provisions since 1947, though doesn't guarantee the leave is paid, nor the number of days available, while Indonesia, South Korea, Zambia and several states in Mexico also have menstrual leave policies in place.

In Australia, some employers have already introduced menstrual and reproductive health leave or flexible work arrangements to support staff experiencing period pain and other reproductive health conditions.

Montana Lower is the founder of INBLUEM, a natural skincare business in regional New South Wales, where she says workplace flexibility and a family-centric approach are built into the company's culture.

Loading...

Employees can access flexible working arrangements, and staff can choose to share their cycle dates through a dedicated team calendar filter.

Ms Lower says recognising the natural fluctuations of the menstrual cycle has benefited both employees and the business.

"When we started making space for that cyclical nature, we noticed an increase in productivity and in how people felt showing up to work," she said.

She's also a strong supporter of universal reproductive leave, arguing menstrual health shouldn't be treated as an illness.

"I disagree with it falling under sick leave because I don't believe cycling women are sick," she said.

"We're undergoing a very necessary process that life depends upon."

Queensland public sector wins reproductive leave

In 2024, the Queensland government gave about 320,000 public sector workers access to 10 days of paid reproductive leave as part of a new agreement with the unions.

Queensland Council of Unions general secretary Jacqueline King says they now want to see it rolled out nationally.

Jacqueline King wants paid reproductive leave to be available nationally. (Supplied)

"Queensland has opened up that doorway for people to actually talk about what are real-life issues and everyday issues for many women, and a recognition that you're not slacking off."

Modelling from the Bankwest Curtin Economics Centre, which was commissioned by a group of unions including the Queensland Council of Unions, found reproductive health issues cost the Australian economy $21.3 billion a year.

It factors in employee absences and the impact of people working through pain at a reduced capacity.

Michelle O'Shea is a researcher in workplace equity at Western Sydney University who, along with colleagues, made a submission to the National Employment Standards (NES) inquiry calling for all Australian workers to receive reproductive leave.

"We've got a situation where women are engaged in the labour market in a way never seen before," Dr O'Shea told triple j hack.

She argues governments ultimately want to keep women in the workforce.

"So what that also means is we're going to have, increasingly, women experiencing things like perimenopause and menopause while they're also negotiating, obviously, paid employment."

Dr O'Shea says it's also important to challenge the idea of the "ideal worker".

"Women's bodies are often thought of as being leaky and problematic. No, they're not. It's just the workplace environments in which many people operate are very inflexible. And a lot of that is because of a discourse of the past."

Could small businesses absorb the costs?

Not everyone thinks legislating reproductive leave is the right way forward.

Liam Jones from the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry says employers understand reproductive health issues can be hard to deal with, but believes a more flexible approach is needed.

"Many small businesses simply can't absorb the extra cost, particularly given they're dealing with a cost-of-doing-business crisis.

"We think a more balanced approach is needed, one that supports people through genuine flexibility and the entitlements that already exist, without bringing new costs onto the businesses that employ them."

A government spokesperson said the National Employment Standards committee was considering all evidence carefully and would make recommendations accordingly.

The government will then consider those recommendations.

title: Rob Hirst's family and friends help finish book honouring Midnight Oil songwriter
text:
There are drummers, and then there was Rob Hirst.

Hitting the drums (and water tank) with precision and force, Hirst was not only the percussive motor driving Midnight Oil, but also the band's key songwriter with his beautiful high vocal harmonies.

His death from pancreatic cancer in January triggered an outpouring of grief around Australia and the world for the loss of a truly one-of-a-kind musician.

About a month after he died, his daughter Lex Hirst took on a difficult but rewarding project to finish the book her dad had been working on prior to his death.

Rob and Lex Hirst. (Supplied: Hardie Grant Publishing)

Rob had spent the previous two years racing against cancer to complete World is Almost at Peace: A Lifetime of Songwriting for Midnight Oil and More.

He was about 85 per cent done when he died.

"I went back to work about a month after Dad died and just did a deep dive straight into this project," Lex said.

"It was amazing actually — I did sit at my desk and cry most days, but in a really cathartic way.

"I had this fear of losing his voice or losing these small parts of him, and then to sit down and read the document from beginning to end, his voice is so well captured.

"It was actually a really helpful thing for me at that particular moment of grieving."

World is Almost at Peace is a journey through Rob's life as a songwriter, moving track by track through every completed and recorded song in his back catalogue.

The cover of Rob Hirst's book World is Almost at Peace. (Supplied: Hardie Grant Publishing)

It takes readers from his first stumbling attempts as a lyricist, through his contributions to Midnight Oil's socially conscious landmark tracks such as Beds Are Burning and Read About It, and on to his other myriad projects, such as with the bands Ghostwriters and Backsliders.

"It opens in the foreword with a little bit that says, 'A confession — some of these early songs were written or co-written by an ambitious Australian teenager with little or no real-world experience. They read like it,'" Lex laughed.

"Going from that through to the politicisation of [Midnight Oil] ... you see the shifts.

"And then you go through to some of the more personal songs, and then the last album that he worked on is his most personal ... because he wrote it while he was sick and someone coming to terms with the end of their life as well.

"That arc I found really interesting to work through."

Midnight Oil, playing at Manly, with Rob Hirst balancing precariously atop his kit. (Supplied: Hardie Grant Publishing)

Spurred on by his wife Lesley Holland, Rob began the project in the knowledge he was not long for the world.

"He was so passionate about getting this out — my dad, he loved to work," Lex said.

"This book was a way, I think, for him to continue to process what it meant to be a songwriter over an entire lifetime.

"I think also because [songwriting] was the last element of music that he was really always able to engage with. Even after he got sick, he was constantly writing and creating, but he couldn't really do a huge amount on the drums.

"So I do think ... part of the reason [for the book] is him claiming his identity as a writer, probably first and foremost.

" We were very careful to stick to his brief, which was he didn't want it to be a drumming book. "

With help from Rob's family, friends, and fellow musicians, Lex said they were able to fill in the gaps her dad had left in the manuscript.

Amid his own anecdotes and some words from his many collaborators, World is Almost at Peace sees the Midnight Oil drummer/singer break down his songwriting to a level rarely seen in these types of books.

Rob Hirst had almost completed his book, World is Almost at Peace, when he died in January.

"It has the songs chronologically in there and then there are notes along the way and artefacts, but he's also broken down who wrote individual lines of songs," she explained.

"So they're colour-coded differently [so you can tell, for example] in Midnight Oil, whether it was him or Jim [Moginie] or Pete [Garrett] who wrote the individual rhyme, line or even word."

World is Almost at Peace ends with Rob's final song, An Upwelling, which is the only song in the book that was never recorded.

"He was writing it still when he died, and he sort of would sing bits to us," Lex said.

"He's actually left chords alongside it, because he likes the idea that someone else would take it and take it out into the world."

The book, she said, is a neat summary of her dad's career.

"This book was created very much, I think, with an idea that, yeah, this is what he was leaving for us all."

title: Judge dismisses Trump lawsuit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein cartoon
text:
A federal judge has thrown out US President Donald Trump's $US10 billion ($14 billion) lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

US District Judge Darrin Gayles dismissed the lawsuit filed in Miami, saying the president was "grasping at straws".

Judge Gayles ruled the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice as required by law and the suit had attempted to "manufacture" flaws in the newspaper's reporting.

The lawsuit against the WSJ was over a story it published last year describing a sexually suggestive letter and drawing that the paper said bore Mr Trump's name and was included in a 2003 album compiled for Epstein's 50th birthday.

The letter was reportedly collected by disgraced British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell as part of a birthday album for Epstein years before he was first arrested in 2006 and subsequently had a falling-out with Mr Trump.

Mr Trump denied writing it and called the story "false, malicious and defamatory".

The case was thrown out "with prejudice", which means it cannot be refiled again and the dismissal is permanent.

A spokesperson for News Corp's Dow Jones (the WSJ's parent) told the WSJ it was pleased with the decision.

A spokesman for Mr Trump's legal team told the WSJ the president would appeal the ruling.

"The president will continue to hold those who mislead the American people with fake news and smears accountable for their actions," the spokesman said.

Trump calls out 'malicious' reporting

The letter bearing Mr Trump's name includes text framed by the outline of what appears to be a hand-drawn naked woman and ends with, "Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret", according to the newspaper.

This image posted Monday, Sept. 8, 2025, on the X account of the Democrats on the House Oversight Committee shows a sexually suggestive birthday note to Jeffrey Epstein alluding to a "wonderful secret" and purportedly signed by President Donald Trump, who has denied sending the note. (X: @OversightDems)

In his lawsuit, Mr Trump called the alleged birthday greeting "fake" and sought $US10 billion for what he called damage to his reputation.

News Corp's Dow Jones defended the accuracy of its July 17, 2025, article.

The lawsuit was one of several Mr Trump has filed in his second term against major media outlets over reporting he has characterised as unfair or false.

In asking Judge Gayles to dismiss the case in September, lawyers for the WSJ and its billionaire owner Rupert Murdoch wrote that the lawsuit threatened to chill the speech of those who publish content that Mr Trump does not like.

Wasn't the case already dismissed?

Yes.

Donald Trump's case, originally filed July 18, 2025 against The Wall Street Journal (WSJ), was thrown out by the same judge, Darrin Gayles, in April of this year.

He said the article did not meet the "actual malice" standard that public figures must clear in defamation.

They must prove not only that a public statement about them was false but also that the media outlet or person who made the statement knew or should have known that it was false.

"This complaint comes nowhere close to this standard," Judge Gayles wrote.

"Quite the opposite."

Trump ordered to sit for deposition in his $14b BBC lawsuit The US president is suing the British broadcaster, alleging it defamed him by splicing together two pieces of his speech made to supporters before they stormed the US Capitol on January 6, 2021.

Mr Trump was then allowed to refile the lawsuit which he did later that month.

According to the amended lawsuit, Mr Trump called Mr Murdoch on July 15, 2025, after WSJ reporters contacted the White House about the story.

"In response, Murdoch stated, 'I will handle it,' which President Trump reasonably interpreted as meaning that Murdoch believed President Trump, and that the article would not be published," the lawsuit says.

Representatives of Dow Jones did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the filing or on the allegation regarding Mr Murdoch.

Dow Jones, which News Corp owns, previously said it had full confidence in the WSJ's reporting and will defend itself in court.

Mr Murdoch is chairman emeritus of News Corp.

How has the case been permanently thrown out?

In the US, a case being thrown out "with prejudice" means it is permanently over and there is no reason to bring it back to court.

In Saturday's ruling, the judge cited the Supreme Court's landmark 1964 ruling in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan.

That decision made it harder for public figures to win libel lawsuits because it requires proof that a media outlet knowingly published something false or showed a reckless disregard for the truth.

“The Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice," Judge Gayles wrote.

"Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false."

The judge also noted that the WSJ's story did not ignore or minimise Mr Trump's denial.

"Rather, it informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it."

Judge Gayles also said several other allegations in the lawsuit did not have merit.

ABC/Wires

title: FBI accuses North Korea of Binance hack
text:
The FBI has accused North Korea of stealing $US6.3 billion n ($6.9 million) in virtual assets from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, in what is thought to be the biggest crypto heist in history.

In a statement, the US bureau said the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the "malicious cyber activity".

On Thursday, $US6.3 billion in bitcoin and other digital currency was stolen from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, in what several crypto experts said bore the hallmarks of a North Korean hack.

The FBI's statement came as Binance offered reassurances it was covering the losses from the hacking attack, saying it has used company funds to buy tokens to replenish 90 per cent of what was stolen.

The FBI made the announcement on Saturday, local time. (Reuters: Nathan Howard)

The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to make sure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins.

"The FBI maintains its commitment to protecting the virtual asset community by identifying, mitigating, and disrupting North Korea's illicit cybercrime and virtual asset theft activities," it said.

It also said its probe found that TraderTraitor was converting stolen assets primarily into a cryptocurrency called Ethereum.

Zhao Changpeng is the founder and chief executive officer of Binance. (Reuters: Benoit Tessier)

The FBI said it expects TraderTraitor would now attempt to convert the assets using de-centralised finance (DeFi) and "instant swap services".

"It is expected these assets will then be further laundered," it said.

They are the same actors behind a $US1.5 billion Bybit hack last year.

'Cat and mouse game' of tracking assets

Crypto expert and chief policy officer at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs Ari Redbord said he expected the hackers would break the stolen assets into pieces and try to launder them through smaller exchanges to evade detection, a process that could unfold over months.

A crypto expert says he expects the hackers will break the stolen assets into pieces and try to launder them. (Unsplash: Executium)

"It's bank robbery, in this case, at the speed of the internet," Mr Redbord said.

"However, we can also track and trace those funds in real time in order to build investigations, to disrupt and to seize back funds.

"It's just this cat and mouse game."

90 per cent of assets recovered, Binance says

On Saturday, Binance said it had enough set aside in the same digital currency that was stolen, to cover 90 per cent of the missing assets.

"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the company said on X.

It said the outstanding 10 per cent consists of tokens that are less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts.

Binance suspended user withdrawals after the hack, but said in its latest update that they were on track to resume Sunday.

Reuters/AFP/AP

title: Fifty years on, Julius Dam continues to sustain outback communities
text:
In 1971, a devastating drought exposed a serious problem in the outback mining city of Mount Isa. Despite having a major dam, the city was running short of water.

Lake Moondarra, built by Mount Isa Mines in 1958 on the Leichhardt River north of town, was Australia's largest, privately-funded water scheme at the time.

But as the city and its mining industry grew, the drought exposed a need for another reliable water source.

The solution was unveiled five years later with the completion of Julius Dam, about 70 kilometres north-east of Mount Isa, at the junction of the Leichhardt River and Paroo Creek.

The North-West Star declared "No more water worries" when Julius Dam was officially commissioned on October 8, 1976. (Supplied: North-West Star)

An engineering solution built for the outback

Constructed by Thiess Brothers, Julius Dam required hundreds of workers, including people from Scotland, England and Ireland, some of whom lived on site with their families.

Building a structure with a 220-metre spillway in remote Queensland had significant challenges.

Hundreds of workers helped construct Julius Dam between 1973 and 1976, overcoming the challenges of building in remote North West Queensland. (Supplied: Sunwater)

Engineers chose a concrete multiple-arch and buttress design that reduced the amount of material needed while maintaining the dam's strength.

The design helped overcome the difficulties of building in the outback, according to current operator Sunwater.

"Because of its remoteness, because of the difficulty of getting materials in, that's the reason they decided to go with that structure," north region general manager of operations, William Weaver said.

Julius Dam's distinctive multiple-arch and buttress design reduced the amount of concrete required for construction. (Supplied: Sunwater)

Sunwater says it remains the only dam of its kind in Queensland.

But another feature caught the attention of University of Queensland geotechnical engineering professor Alexander Scheuermann.

"The first thing I thought when I saw the dam was, 'Where's the spillway?'" he said.

Professor Alexander Scheuermann says Julius Dam's unique design allows floodwater to flow directly over its structure. (Supplied: Alexander Scheuermann)

Unlike dams with a separate spillway, Julius Dam's concrete, 18m wide arches allow excess water to flow directly over the structure.

"When the water rises higher than the dam is, it simply overtops the dam without harming the structure," Professor Scheuermann said.

Julius Dam: By the numbers Construction: 1973–1976

1973–1976 Dam wall length: 399 metres

399 metres Maximum height: 34 metres

34 metres Spillway length: 220 metres

220 metres Span of each arch: 18.3 metres

18.3 metres Concrete used: 45,000 cubic metres

45,000 cubic metres Storage capacity: 107,500 megalitres (Sunwater)

107,500 megalitres (Sunwater) Design: Multiple-arch and buttress

Multiple-arch and buttress Main contractor: Thiess Brothers Sources: Original Julius Dam engineering plaque and Sunwater.

A reliable water source for the North West

Julius Dam can hold 107,500 megalitres of water, equivalent to about one-fifth of Sydney Harbour's volume.

While originally developed to supplement Mount Isa's water supply, its role has expanded over the past five decades.

The 113-kilometre North West Queensland Water Pipeline, completed in 1998, supplies mining operations including the Ernest Henry copper and gold mine near Cloncurry.

Another 38km pipeline was completed in 2010 following a drought, providing Cloncurry with an additional year-round water supply.

Lake Moondarra remains Mount Isa's main water source, with Julius Dam providing supplementary water when needed.

Julius Dam's built-in spillway allows excess water to flow directly over its concrete arches during periods of heavy rainfall. (Supplied: Sunwater)

Despite the region's long dry periods, Mr Weaver said Julius Dam had spilled every year for the past decade.

He attributed its reliability to seasonal monsoonal and cyclonic rainfall regularly replenishing the Leichhardt River catchment.

"What Lake Julius does is it gives you that real assurance and real surety of supply," he said.

"And that's allowed Mount Isa and its industry to grow."

William Weaver says Julius Dam remains a vital water source for North West Queensland. (Supplied: Sunwater )

Built to last another 50 years

While Julius Dam has operated for five decades, Professor Scheuermann said ongoing maintenance would be essential to its future.

He said dams could remain operational for more than a century, but changing rainfall patterns, extreme weather and future water demand would need to be considered as infrastructure aged.

"So you need to have the skilled labour and also the engineers who are able to assess the safety of the dam."

Julius Dam spilling before construction was completed in 1976. (Supplied: Sunwater)

Mr Weaver said a seven-person team based in Cloncurry operated and maintained the dam and its associated pipelines.

For a structure tucked away in a remote stretch of the Leichhardt River, its contribution reaches far beyond the water it holds.

"It's one of those little hidden gems that most people don't even know exists because it's tucked away in the middle of nowhere," Mr Weaver said.

"So it's a hidden gem, but it certainly does a great job."

title: Country town reliant on backpackers warns visa changes will cripple business
text:
In Paul Fowler's country pub, more than half a dozen backpackers make up over 70 per cent of his workforce.

Italian travellers keep business ticking over from the front of house all the way through to his busy kitchen.

It is a similar situation at many businesses across Manjimup, 290 kilometres south of Perth in southern Western Australia, with the tourism and agricultural centre heavily reliant on backpacker labour.

Seventy per cent of the staff at Paul Fowler's pub are backpackers. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

Both Mr Fowler and his workers have backed calls to scrap the federal government's controversial changes to Australia's working holiday visa program.

"It's only going to make things harder, and it takes away our ability to function," he said.

Before the working holiday visa changes were announced, Mr Fowler bought a second pub in the neighbouring town of Pemberton, which he planned to staff with backpackers.

Viola Argenta, Ilaria Dalla Valeria and Mattia Ballarini all work at a pub in Manjimup. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

Mr Fowler said that business was now under threat.

"We probably go through 50 to 80 workers a year, all backpacking workers, and so without the backpacking staff, we won't have a workforce here at all," he said.

" We could have more workers now if we could get them, but they're not here. "

Paul Fowler says his pub in Manjimup couldn't run without backpacker labour. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

The federal government's decision to initially slow down visa applications in August was heavily criticised by farming and regional communities across the country.

The decision to allocate fewer second and third-year visa extensions prompted WA's Premier Roger Cook to ask federal Immigration Minister Tony Burke to reconsider the restrictions.

Manjimup is a regional hub for tourism and agriculture. (ABC South West: Andrew Williams)

A spokesperson for the Department of Home Affairs said the reduction would ensure the program's long-term sustainability, and it would work with affected industries to access the labour they need.

Back in Manjimup, those impacted say the move fails to account for the benefits backpackers provide beyond their first year.

Roberto Spadotto wants to build a life in Manjimup. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

Roberto Spadotto came to Manjimup to work as a farmhand, picking avocados and broccoli as part of his visa obligations.

After completing his 88 days and being granted an extension, he started managing Mr Fowler's pub along with his partner Giulia Colombo, whom he met while completing his farm work.

"That's where I met Giulia … one of the worst and best days of my life because picking broccoli is very tough, but I enjoyed it and I had a good outcome," he said.

After spending about four years in the region, the Italian couple were hoping to put down roots.

"I love the area, love the region, never really thought about moving somewhere else," he said.

"And now we're planning to stay, settle, and build a new life here in Australia."

Backpackers shipping out

Fellow Italian traveller Valerie Casto completed her farm work in a seedling nursery, before starting work as a chef once her visa was extended.

Valerie Casto says second and third-year visa extensions incentivise backpackers to do hard jobs. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

She said the incoming changes were turning some of her friends off coming to Australia.

"Half a year of a farm job can be very, very hard," Ms Castro said.

"And some people don't know if it's worth it, if at the end the visa is not granted."

Gavin Booth says backpacker workers are already leaving Australia. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

It is an experience all too familiar for truffle farmer Gavin Booth, who produces the valuable fungus on a property in neighbouring Pemberton.

He relies on backpackers for sporadic and seasonal work.

"We had a girl who's worked for us for a couple of years, a French backpacker, and she was on her third year visa when she found out she would have to go into a 5,000-space lottery," he said.

"She just said, 'Stuff this, I don't want to do this' and left.

"She was happy to come here and earn the money, to spend the money in this economy, and now she's left for Bali."

title: Passengers give their verdicts on new Spirit of Tasmania
text:
The sky was clear and the sea calm when Spirit of Tasmania V arrived in Devonport at 6:19am on Sunday morning.

For a channel known for baring its teeth, Bass Strait had been kind to the passengers and crew.

This calls for a toast! (ABC News)

About 12 hours earlier, guests took selfies and drank wine on the pristine deck as the new ship left Geelong for its maiden passenger voyage.

As a guitarist wove through the crowd, dignitaries were singing the vessel's praises.

"We've stayed the course, and we've got it done," Tasmanian premier Jeremy Rockliff told ABC reporters, who were invited on the inaugural crossing.

Alison Jarman with Jeremy Rockliff, ahead of the inaugural voyage. (ABC News)

Standing beside the premier was an emotional Devonport mayor Alison Jarman, who likened the Spirit of Tasmania brand to the Sydney Opera House.

"She's iconic … and so are these two ships to our state," she said.

The view from the deck as Spirit of Tasmania IV heads into Bass Strait. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Chris Carbone and Alison Jarman pose for a selfie. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

The new Spirits, which were beset by delays and cost blowouts, were built by Finnish company Rauma Marine Constructions.

"It's a historic moment for us … a beautiful collaboration," said the Finnish ambassador to Australia, Arto Haapea.

" It's a beautiful story. "

Arto Haapea was there to help celebrate. (ABC News)

Some of the food on display. (ABC News)

There are screens to keep the kids entertained. (ABC News)

Ship enthusiasts were not going to miss the historic occasion.

Mitchell Bruce, creator of the Ferries in Tasmania website, said he had been passionate about the Spirits for decades.

"Growing up in Tassie, going across on the original Spirit … it sparked an interest inside me," he said.

" It's great that we have these things from another part of the world that are servicing the island of Tasmania. "

Ferry enthusiast Mitchell Bruce was there to mark the occasion. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

The view of the vehicle gantry during embarkation, as seen by Mitchell Bruce. (Ferries of Tasmania: Mitchell Bruce)

A view of one of the lounge areas, as photographed by Mitchell Bruce. (Ferries of Tasmania: Mitchell Bruce)

A peek inside a cabin aboard Spirit of Tasmania IV, as photographed by Mitchell Bruce. (Ferries of Tasmania: Mitchell Bruce)

For many on board, the historic crossing was a journey home.

Celeste Ackerly, accompanied by her child and two pet dogs, was returning to Tasmania and had initially been unaware that she had booked on Spirit V's maiden crossing.

"It's pretty cool to know this is the first time," she said.

Celeste Ackerly travelled with her dogs. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Brian Munday was capping off a mainland road trip with a memorable night at sea.

"We've been all up Queensland, three and a half months on the road, and now we're heading home," he told the ABC.

" It's a nice ship. The finished product is good. "

Brian Munday liked what he saw of the ship. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Sweety Neik, from Melbourne, was embarking on her first Tasmanian adventure, with Cradle Mountain and Hobart's Salamanca Market high on her to-do list.

"It's very exciting. I was looking forward to [October] 31," she said.

" I want to go and see how good Tasmania is. "

Sweety Neik is excited to see the sights of Tasmania. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

As the Sun slowly rose above Bass Strait this morning, with the north-west Tasmanian coast coming into view, Mr Rockliff and Transport Minister Kerry Vincent addressed the media.

"This is a pretty iconic moment, and I think everybody on board felt that last night," Mr Vincent said.

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff with Minister of Infrastructure and Transport Kerry Vincent. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

The grand occasion called for roving music on the deck. (ABC News: Sandy Powell)

There is hope that November 1, 2026, will mark a "new dawn" for a brand that has spent years in the headlines for the wrong reasons.

"This project certainly had its challenges," the premier said.

" But some very capable people picked up the mantle and got it done. "

Sandy Powell and Mackenzie Heard were invited on the inaugural sailing.

An upsizing couple paid $2.14 million for a renovated Alexandria terrace with a rooftop garden at auction on Saturday, beating two others and still securing a discount to the reserve. The three-bedroom home at 182 Henderson Road had a kitchen and dining area that led out to a courtyard and then a smart rooftop terrace for entertaining, set above the garage. The property was one of 985 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 48 per cent from 564 reported results throughout the week, while 208 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. The clearance rate has edged up from the low it reached last week, when the preliminary result was 45 per cent, its lowest all year. But it remains far below the 60 per cent threshold that indicates a market balanced between buyers and sellers, and suggests prices are still falling.

The buyers are a young couple from Redfern upsizing from a unit who like the lock-up garage, a rare feature in the neighbourhood, Stoker said, adding they also like the area and its proximity to transport options.

Four parties registered for the home, listed with a price guide of $1.25 million, and all four participated. Bidding began at $1.15 million and was a little slow at the start as buyers hesitated. A public secondary school in Melbourne’s south-east has won the approval of parents, defying a trend for those on the city’s fringe to record lower parental satisfaction scores due to ageing facilities and student bullying. An analysis of the annual opt-in survey of more than 300 government-run secondary schools across the state, found Stonnington had the most satisfied parents – giving the schools an average rating of 89.2 per cent. Average satisfaction scores are similarly high for schools in Glen Eira (85 per cent) and Port Phillip (82.6 per cent). By contrast, Cardinia (55.8 per cent), Nillumbik (59.1 per cent) and Melton (61.5 per cent) were on average home to the Melbourne schools with the least satisfied parents with in 2025. While schools in growth corridors tended to have lower scores, the area of Casey rose above. The average parental satisfaction of schools there is 72.9 per cent, driven up by select-entry Nossal High School (96.3) and Cranbourne West Secondary College (97.6 per cent).

Advertisement

Still, experts say the figures highlight the stress public schools in growth areas are under, and the need to ensure government funding and services back up the commitment of teachers. National Growth Areas chief executive Bronwen Clark said communities on the city’s fringe were grappling with a number of pressures as the population expanded. “I think that all plays into a catching-up process, that organic growth of transport systems, school growth, maturity in the school community takes time,” she said. “It may well be that part of the frustration for parents is the transport to get their kids to school, and the traffic and the congestion. And it may well be that some secondary schools have a vast number of portable classrooms.” Statewide, schools that ran from prep to year 12 were ranked lower (70.1 per cent) than standalone secondary schools (74.1 per cent), with P-12 schools more commonly located in regional areas with lower satisfaction levels.

Advertisement

Regionally, parents gave the most positive ratings to schools in Pyrenees Shire (93.8 per cent), and the lowest in Wodonga (48.2 per cent). Closer to the city centre, parents rated two Melbourne schools with scores of 100 per cent satisfaction: Box Hill Senior Secondary College, in Melbourne’s east, which has 282 students, and Bindjiroo Yaluk Community School, which has just 79 students across campuses in Richmond and Coburg. Cranbourne West Secondary College principal Rob Duncan (back middle) with his 2025 VCE high achievers. Joe Armao Cranbourne West Secondary College principal Rob Duncan said the Casey area school’s high parental satisfaction correlated with other strong results, across VCE scores, student engagement and strong management of bullying.

Advertisement

“Because we’re a reasonably multicultural community, we obviously try to make sure we’ve got staff who the parents feel that they can communicate with,” Duncan said, adding teachers spoke several different languages. “We make ourselves as accessible as possible when parents have concerns, that’s the entire leadership team. And we have a genuine focus on positive outcomes for kids.” Parents Victoria chief executive Gail McHardy said that while families could face different educational experiences depending on where they lived, survey results should be used as a starting point and “not a definitive verdict on a school or its staff”. Related Article Education The Melbourne schools with the most portable buildings and the impact on students “Parental satisfaction reflects many factors: the quality of relationships between schools and families, student learning, safety, bullying, mental health and wellbeing, disability inclusion, teacher availability, facilities and access to specialist support … But every school is different, and we should not assume geography alone explains the results,” she said.

Advertisement

“Parents in growth corridors may be navigating additional pressures around school capacity, infrastructure and access to support services. These are system-planning issues, not a reflection of the commitment of local school communities.” In Cardinia Shire, the average school’s parent satisfaction result was 55.8 per cent, the lowest across metropolitan areas. Parents at one local secondary school told The Age that while they were happy with the school’s teachers and buildings (which recently received $11.3 million for upgrades and modernisation), they were concerned about bullying and student suspensions. “I’ve found the teachers have been really good,” said Jayde Valsveld, who attended the school herself and has sent four children there. “If there’s been any issues, they’ve been involved. And now with all the new buildings going in, they’re way overdue.” Though parents reported some students being suspended multiple times without a change in behaviour, Valsveld said: “With every school, the bullying could be improved; the way bullies are handled discipline-wise.”

Advertisement

A spokesperson for the Department of Education said the school treated all allegations of bullying seriously and addressed incidents with appropriate and proportionate consequences. The organisers of Australia’s biggest triathlon have been forced to cancel the swim leg of the race for the first time in the event’s history after multiple shark sightings over the weekend. The Noosa Triathlon is the largest Olympic-distance triathlon event in the world, drawing more than 13,000 competitors to the Sunshine Coast town over the five-day festival. In an update posted to the event’s Instagram, organisers warned Sunday’s swim course would be altered “due to marine life sightings” which closed Noosa’s Main Beach for periods on Saturday. The Noosa Triathlon usually begins with a 1500-metre swim off Noosa’s Main Beach. They hoped an “M-shaped” swim bringing athletes closer to the shore would allay safety concerns, but an updated post published Sunday morning stated “due to marine life present … the swim will not be taking place”.

Advertisement

Noosa Triathlon spokesman Craig Heydon said the decision was made to cancel the swim altogether as there had been a number of shark sightings over the last few weeks and days, with some animals sighted within the race’s swim perimeter. “[The race has] a 1.5 kilometre swim, which goes a couple of 100 metres offshore, and the animals [sighted] were within that space,” Heydon explained. “So the decision was made that it wasn’t safe to put swimmers in the water today.” This is the first time the swim leg has been cancelled in the event’s 43-year history.

Advertisement

“We obviously had quite a lot of rain in recent weeks, which might have been part of what led to having them in the water,” he said. “But from an event perspective, the team was able to pivot really quickly, and our athletes are still out on course now and having a great day.” Competitors in the event’s elite race started at 6.15 am on Sunday, swapping the 1500-metre swim with a five-kilometre run, followed by a 40-kilometre ride and a 10-kilometre run. Related Article Olympics How much will it cost getting to Brisbane 2032? A legend’s daughter and Olympic hopeful reveals For the age group athletes who make up the majority of the race, the swim component was swapped for a short beach run.

Advertisement

“[Athletes] put a lot of training into these events, so they would have liked to be able to do a triathlon,” Heydon said. “But they’re certainly very understanding of the reasons why the decision was made today.” Despite the disruptions, Australian triathlete Matt Hauser defended his Noosa Triathlon title, claiming victory on Sunday with a one hour, 39 minutes and 34 second finish. Australia’s Matthew Hauser competes during the men’s individual triathlon competition at the 2024 Summer Olympics, AP “You have to keep adapting to situations and changes, and we had to make of it what we could and the crowd got a kick out of it,” Hauser said of the 45-minute notice of the race changes.

Advertisement

“It’s Noosa, you have to do the race justice and give it a crack.“ Fellow Paris Olympian Luke Willian finished in second place (1:42:59), followed by US racer John Reed. Fellow Paris Olympian Natalie Van Coevorden claimed the women’s title, surprising herself in what was her first race over the distance since the 2024 event. With AAP

Exclusive TechnologySpace Europe’s answer to Elon Musk’s Starlink wants to build satellites in Australia David Swan November 1, 2026 — 1:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Helsinki: A Finnish satellite maker says it could help Australia build its own alternative to Elon Musk’s Starlink, made locally and owned by Australians. ReOrbit, which assembles communications satellites for defence customers inside a former Ford car factory in Helsinki, wants to set up manufacturing in Australia with local companies and the government. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carrying 53 Starlink satellites. (Craig Bailey/Florida Today via AP) AP “I’m very interested personally, making this happen in Australia,” chief commercial officer Markus Räikkönen told this masthead in an interview. He plans to visit in February. The pitch arrives as Australia leans harder on satellites it does not control. From next year, the Universal Outdoor Mobile Obligation requires the mobile carriers to provide basic outdoor voice and text coverage through a low-earth-orbit satellite partner, so a phone with no tower in range can still send a message.

Advertisement

ReOrbit chief commercial officer Markus Räikkönen. The Australian Telecommunications Alliance, the industry’s peak body, says that market “does not currently provide any competitive options”. Telstra and Optus have both signed with Elon Musk’s Starlink for satellite-to-phone services. In late October, Musk said SpaceX had restricted Ukraine’s Starlink service, accusing its military of breaching the terms by using it for “offensive drone strikes”, which Ukrainian officials dispute. Ukraine says the problems hampered its defensive operations for more than a week. Musk had earlier denied deliberately throttling the service, which was restored after US President Donald Trump said he had told Musk to “put it back”. Räikkönen said it matters little to someone shopping online whose satellite carries the signal. For defence, he said, it is “extremely important who controls the satellite connectivity”. “Can somebody turn it off? Can somebody slow it down?” Sovereignty used to mean leasing a reserved slice of capacity on another operator’s satellite, he said. Governments now want the whole system. “I want to own my satellites, my ground station. I want to operate the satellite,” he said, describing what customers ask for, with data landing in their own country and “no restrictions or kill switch” outside it.

Advertisement

Australia would need more of them than most. Finland could cover its critical communications with a single geostationary satellite, which sits fixed about 36,000 kilometres above the equator, Räikkönen said. “For Australia it’s a massive land area,” he said, and several would be needed. Elon Musk’s Starlink has agreements with both Telstra and Optus. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson A sovereign version of Starlink, using satellites about 550 kilometres up, would need a constellation of about 600 to 1000 satellites for Australia, he said, though a service could start with fewer. ReOrbit would act as the systems integrator and hand over the know-how, he said. “With a company like ReOrbit we could actually do it in Australia and everything could be owned by locals,” he said. One of ReOrbit’s satellites.

Advertisement

Australia has tried this before. In 2024, the Defence Department cancelled JP9102, a $6.9 billion sovereign military satellite communications system built around new geostationary satellites, a year and a half after awarding the contract to Lockheed Martin Australia. ReOrbit was founded in 2019 and has about 160 staff, adding more than 10 a month, Räikkönen said. Its biggest investors are Finnish pension funds, including Varma and Elo. That helps in defence sales, Räikkönen said, because governments wary of choosing between American and Chinese suppliers can buy Finnish without upsetting anyone. “If you buy from Finland, nobody cares.” Related Article Opinion

Aviation Starlink’s growing influence has one big point of failure Chris Zappone Senior reporter, aviation Chief executive Sethu Saveda Suvanam has pitched ReOrbit as an affordable alternative to Starlink for countries that cannot build their own satellites, TechCrunch reported when the company raised €45 million ($71.7 million) last year, in what the site described as a record round for a European space start-up. He said it had signed a contract worth “some hundreds of millions” with one country and memorandums of understanding with others. ReOrbit’s first satellite, which runs artificial intelligence on board to analyse images before sending them down, is due to launch in February on a SpaceX rideshare flight. Räikkönen said whether SpaceX keeps launching rivals’ satellites is “completely on them to decide”, though he expects it to, because the business helps pay for its rockets. The launch is set for the same month as his Australian trip.

NationalNSWCity life The prime slice of coastal Sydney with roads, paths – and almost no homes David Barwell November 1, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
