When plans were first unveiled to develop a prime stretch of coastal land in Sydney’s south-east into hundreds of new homes, confidence appeared high, as construction crews got to work building all the roads, footpaths and residential lots in preparation for an influx of new residents. But more than a decade later, only a handful of homes have been completed, the footpaths are largely empty, and the streets are frequented mainly by the occasional street sweeper, cyclist and parents taking their teenage children for supervised learner driver lessons. An aerial view of the Little Bay site. Sam Mooy Amid debate over new housing in Sydney’s eastern suburbs, the site’s owner and Australia’s richest property developer, Harry Triguboff, is embarking on a new plan to develop the land after three previous proposals to build thousands of apartments failed to gain planning approval and faced strong community opposition. Through his company, Meriton, Triguboff has submitted a new proposal for 505 homes in buildings of up to five storeys on the coastal site overlooking Little Bay Beach and the fairways of The Coast Golf Club.

Advertisement

The plan, which includes an initial stage of 100 homes, three of which would be affordable dwellings, received initial support this month from the NSW government’s Housing Delivery Authority, a planning body established to boost housing supply through streamlined assessments that bypass local councils. Related Article Development ‘Like some sort of giant, concrete zombie’: Meriton makes new bid for redevelopment of Little Bay The proposal marks a significant departure from the scale of Meriton’s previous plans, which included an application for 1900 apartments rejected by the Sydney Eastern City Planning Panel in 2021, a rezoning bid for 1600 homes in 2023 and an application for 2600 apartments across two 27-storey towers last year. Instead, the latest proposal brings the development closer to the scale of an approved masterplan Meriton inherited when it acquired the site for $245 million in 2017, which permitted up to 450 homes in buildings of up to five storeys. While Meriton declined to comment on its latest proposal, the company has consistently maintained its commitment to developing the site.

Advertisement

The change in scale has been cautiously welcomed by some residents including Olde Lorenzen, a founding member of community group Save Little Bay which has spent years campaigning against high-rise development at the site. “When residents bought their homes here, they did so expecting a mix of low and medium density housing in the area, not thousands of units in buildings up to 27 storeys,” he said. Local resident Olde Lorenzen pictured at the Little Bay site. Louise Kennerley Lorenzen said residents wanted assurances that the state government’s planning pathway would not pave the way for further increases in density. “It’s a step in the right direction, but our concern is that Meriton is using a state-significant pathway and we’ll be looking for clear assurances that what begins as 505 homes doesn’t become the start of a push for even greater density.

Advertisement

“We’re not anti-development, we just want sustainable development for the site, which is in a sensitive coastal environment.” The prolonged vacancy of the site had also created problems for nearby residents, he said, due to issues including trespassing and antisocial behaviour. Little Bay Cove has footpaths, roads – but no homes. Sam Mooy “Even though it’s fenced off, it’s regularly accessed by cars, residents, and trespassers,” he said. “There’s a playground on there that is falling apart, the grass is overgrown, we’ve had issues with overflowing bins and vermin, and there’s crime and drug trading going on down there at night. It’s definitely not in a good state.”

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

NSW Votes ‘Not another suburb for luxury housing’: Liberals to unveil Long Bay housing plan Last week, the NSW Coalition opposition announced plans to close the Long Bay Correctional Complex, located about 200 metres north of Little Bay Cove, and redevelop the site for 12,000 homes if elected in March 2027. NSW Planning Minister Paul Scully dismissed the proposal as a “fantasy”, arguing it would cost taxpayers billions of dollars and create excessive density without adequate infrastructure. But he expressed support for the Little Bay development. “It is always good to see underutilised land being activated for new housing,” Scully said.

Advertisement

“From downsizers to families and young people, everyone should have the option to live in the community they choose.” He stressed, however, that the Housing Delivery Authority’s initial support did not guarantee approval, with the proposal still subject to merit-based assessment and community consultation. An artist impression of the housing plan for the site in 2019. Maroubra Labor MP Michael Daley, who has previously criticised Meriton’s larger development plans, also welcomed the reduction in building heights. “If Meriton’s current application broadly represents what was represented in the master plan, that would be a good result,” he said.

Advertisement

“What I don’t want to see is them gaining an approval and then coming back and asking for multiple changes.” Related Article NSW State Parliament ‘A fantasy’: Labor attacks Coalition’s 12,000-home Long Bay plan Randwick Mayor Clare Willington criticised the use of the Housing Delivery Authority pathway, warning it would remove local oversight and “take planning decisions out of the council’s hands.” “Little Bay is a community, not a blank canvas for developers. They deserve a guarantee that a modest proposal today won’t become something very different tomorrow,” she said. Long-time resident Peter Fagan said while lower building heights were a positive compromise, local infrastructure remained a pressing concern.

Advertisement

“Adding another 505 homes will put enormous pressure on roads that are already heavily congested, as well as schools and hospitals,” Fagan said. “Sydney needs more homes, but it also needs responsible planning. The two should go hand in hand.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important stories. Sign up for our Morning Edition newsletter.

The new Fremantle Traffic Bridge, named Walyalup Bridge, has officially opened. Pedestrians were first on the bridge for the festivities at 9am, with a local pipe band and dancers providing a show. Heather McNeill State government ministers, locals, business owners and media gathered on Saturday morning for the official unveiling of the new bridge, with Minister for Transport Rita Saffioti leading the ribbon cutting ceremony. Thousands of pedestrians gathered just after 9am to cross the bridge on Sunday morning, and it will be later opened to traffic. The old Fremantle Traffic Bridge was closed in February, with the new structure originally tipped to open in the first half of 2027. However, fast-tracked construction has enabled it to open early.

Advertisement

The new bridge has the same number of traffic lanes as the old bridge, but has a higher clearance for boats and wider pedestrian lanes. It also updates the old 86-year-old timber framing, with cantilevers and cable stay supports. The state government said construction had since provided more than 1400 jobs. However with the speed of construction came a hefty price tag, with the original cost of the new bridge jumping from $430 million to $596 million in this year’s state budget. Saffioti said at the opening on Sunday the project had been worth the effort.

Advertisement

“Opening it ahead of schedule is an incredible achievement for everyone involved, and I congratulate the entire project team for their innovation and commitment to delivering it as quickly as possible,” she said. “Thank you to the local families, residents, businesses, schools and freight operators who have all played their part to keep the road network moving while we built this spectacular new bridge.” Throughout the bridge’s construction, some Fremantle businesses said they had felt the sting of the closures. Cellarbrations on Canning Highway closed after 17 years in business due to losing customers during the building, while other businesses reported a significant decline in profits and foot traffic due to roadworks. Member for Fremantle Simone McGurk also thanked her constituents for their patience, while Member for Bicton Lisa O’Malley said she acknowledged it had been difficult for some businesses to get through the closure period.

Advertisement

“We know delivering landmark projects like this causes disruption and I can’t thank our community enough for the patience they’ve shown,” O’Malley said. Related Article Perth business ‘A lot of people are sad’: Freo businesses struggle over bridge woes “Residents and businesses in the Bicton electorate and beyond have played an important part in keeping traffic on our roads moving as smoothly possible. Now it’s time to celebrate this iconic new gateway to Fremantle that will be a part of our community’s story for generations to come.” Road access to and from Fremantle via Canning Highway will be re-opened now the bridge is up and running, and Beach Street will also be back open to traffic. Federal Member for Fremantle Josh Wilson said it was important the new bridge had elements of the port city’s long history incorporated into its design.

Advertisement

“Walyalup Bridge is a brilliant addition to our working port, with a name and design that shape Fremantle’s future by respecting its deep cultural and industrial heritage,” he said. “Our community helped shape this project and showed extraordinary patience through its construction, and it is especially fitting that we can open it early by walking across it together.” The bridge has some remaining works to be completed including a lighting test, but is now open to traffic. Some of the timber preserved from the original traffic bridge has been used to build a walkway under the new Walyalup structure, and designers have also kept the brass lantern orbs previously used to light the way for drivers in their same spot. They will still be lit every night.

In this Melbourne Cup Briefing, your wrap of racing news: Injured jockey Harry Coffey is sweating on last-minute medical clearance to take his place in Tuesday’s $10.2 million Melbourne Cup.

Joseph O’Brien’s racing manager Kevin Blake has called for emergencies to become part of the Melbourne Cup after stewards scratched Defiantly on Saturday due to concerns about his gait. Danny Russell

Injured jockey Harry Coffey is sweating on last-minute medical clearance to take his place in Tuesday’s $10.2 million Melbourne Cup. Coffey is booked to partner Ciaron Maher’s lightweight fancy Shockletz in the 3200-metre staying test, but is in a race against the clock to recover from a suspected broken collarbone. Harry Coffey (right) on his way back to the mounting yard. Getty Images Connections said Coffey underwent a small procedure on Sunday and was waiting on his doctor to determine whether his injuries were stable enough to ride.

Advertisement

The 31-year-old father of two took a heavy tumble in the second-last race on Derby Day, sending a shockwave across the Flemington crowd. Racegoers feared for his safety as images on the big screen showed Coffey being catapulted into the air after his mount Pondalowie clipped heels and fell. “He has not been ruled in, he has not been ruled out,” Coffey’s manager Dean Hawkes said of the Cup ride on Sunday. The 2024 Caulfield Cup-winning hoop’s ability to cope with pain was evident after Saturday’s mid-race fall. He pulled himself to his feet and walked back to the mounting yard, cradling his arm, before taking part in a stewards’ inquiry. He was then taken to hospital.

Advertisement

Pondalowie was captured by a clerk of the course in the Flemington straight after the scary incident. The six-year-old mare was cleared of injury by vets. The fall happened at the 500m mark and had officials on high alert, following a horse death during the Caulfield Cup earlier this month. After speaking to Coffey, stewards released a report clearing all riders of any blame. “It was established that when the tempo quickened, Pondalowie, despite the efforts of Coffey, shifted in slightly when laying in, resulting in Pondalowie clipping the heels of Cilacap and falling,” stewards said. Maher and Shockletz’s connections will be anxiously awaiting Coffey’s call in case they need to find a replacement rider for the Cup third favourite.

Advertisement

“We’ll give Harry every opportunity and if he can’t do it we’ll find someone else,” Maher said at the Melbourne Cup barrier draw. “It’s a legitimate chance, so anybody would be disappointed if they were riding that horse and they weren’t able to [through injury].” Lightweight jockey Michael Dee has put his hand up for the Shockletz gig if Coffey is ruled out. He gave up his ride on mare Strictly Business, which will be ridden by Dean Yendall. ‘I don’t feel that’s good enough’: International crack at Melbourne Cup technology

Advertisement

Peter Ryan

Joseph O’Brien’s racing manager Kevin Blake has called for emergencies to become part of the Melbourne Cup after stewards scratched Defiantly on Saturday due to concerns about his gait. The stewards had to make the decision three days out from the race due to the need to lock in the field of 24 at 4.30pm on Saturday, despite the fact the horse may have made the necessary improvement in the remaining two days to take his place. Kevin Blake (left) suggested the technology used for the Melbourne Cup needed to be updated. Getty Images Emergencies are considered impossible because betting technology can’t handle late inclusions to a field of 24. It means if there are late scratchings between 4.30pm Saturday and the race start, fewer runners will race rather than the next qualified horses in the order of entry being granted a start.

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

Melbourne Cup Racing dodges another nightmare after mid-race fall; Derby Day trainer charged by stewards “We know it’s rigorous, we know it’s tough, and so we’re not going to cry about [the decision]. We’re all big boys and girls, but probably the main takeaway from it is they probably need to sort out their emergency situation,” Blake said. “I’m a guest here so I don’t want to be telling people what to do, but for the reason to be that the technology can’t cope with more than 24 runners in 2026 … I don’t feel that’s good enough.” Defiantly’s withdrawal gives stablemate Kizlyar a start, meaning the O’Brien stable still has five runners – but it robs the race of a natural leader, with the four-year-old gelding a noted frontrunner. Blake said the jockey Dylan Browne McMonagle, who had been booked to ride Defiantly, would now jump on Sons And Lovers, who was the best drawn of their five starters with barrier three.

Advertisement

He said local jockeys James McDonald and Craig Williams would need to weave some magic to their mounts Trustyourinstinct and James J Braddock in a good spot after they drew barriers 18 and 24 respectively. Related Melbourne Cup Pick your winners with our 2026 Melbourne Cup sweep McDonald is the in-form jockey after an exhilarating Derby Day where he won four races including the Derby and Trustyourinstinct is sure to win support due to his presence in the saddle. “James is going to have to work his magic to get in and get cover [and] get him racing efficiently, but he is a very classy horse unexposed to the trip,” Blake said. “[He] looks to have a leading chance in the book, so you just hope he gets a kind spin from the draw.”

Advertisement

Last year’s runner-up Goodie Two Shoes is said to be in better form than last season and is expected to carry big bets from his owner J.P. McManus. Blake also talked up Kizlyar’s chances despite his disappointing run in the Moonee Valley Cup, which became a sit and sprint at the finish. Defiantly may run in the Queen Elizabeth Stakes on Saturday as a consolation, with O’Brien due to fly in from the Breeders’ Cup, which is raced in the US, on Monday. Meanwhile at Werribee, Ethan Brown was pleased with Point of Law’s work on Sunday when he visited the horse he rode to victory in the Geelong Cup. Ryan to front stewards inquiry Danny Russell

Trainer Nick Ryan is expected to front a Racing Victoria stewards inquiry on Monday on a charge of possessing syringes containing a synthetic EPO.

Advertisement

Stewards raided Ryan’s Flemington stables on Derby Day morning and allegedly found syringes in the glove box of his car containing Darbepoetin Alfa – a man-made stimulating agent that mimics a natural hormone. Darbepoetin Alfa is listed as a prohibited substance under the rules of racing. As a result, Ryan’s two runners on Derby Day – Doubt Time and Anglais – were scratched. Stewards will seek further evidence from the former jockey at Monday’s hearing after he reserved his plea on Saturday. The hearing will be closed. Stewards have the power to suspend Ryan until the charge against him is heard if they believe his case prejudices the “image, interests, integrity or welfare of racing”. They will also decide on Monday whether Ryan can run last-start winner Terrortorian in the second race at Flemington on Melbourne Cup Day.

The biggest crypto hack in history began with a rehearsal. As trading hummed along on Binance, hackers were quietly running sequences of code on accounts they controlled on the Ethereum blockchain — just a couple of dollars or so at a time. According to cybersecurity analysts, they were testing a program designed to seize control of accounts owned by the world’s largest crypto exchange and smuggle their contents elsewhere. Just after 4pm (New York time) on Thursday, they attacked. Binance, the largest crypto exchange in the world, was hit by a massive hack late last week. Getty Images In short order, the infiltrators drained more than $US6 billion ($8.9 billion) from wallets across at least four different blockchains, setting off a worldwide effort to contain the damage.

From New York to Abu Dhabi and Kyiv, security researchers and Binance executives scrambled to trace the stolen money, freeze accounts and understand how the attackers had breached the exchange and pulled off a heist that has shaken confidence in the crypto industry as it tries to earn greater acceptance in finance’s mainstream. “It’s the largest bank robbery in human history,” said Ari Redbord, global head of policy and government affairs at TRM Labs, a blockchain analytics firm. Redbord’s firm was one of several that mobilised after the attack started. “I literally haven’t slept and I haven’t stopped.” Related Article Cryptocurrencies ‘Biggest hack in history’: Crypto giant freezes assets after $8.9b heist As Binance publicly said it could easily reimburse any losses from the hack on Friday, employees were privately expressing doubts to one another that they’d be paid bonuses this year, according to people familiar with the matter.

The crypto industry is no stranger to malevolent actors. Only a month ago, cryptocurrency exchange Bitget was subject to a cyberattack that drained $US388 million. In February 2025, hackers stole nearly $US1.5 billion from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit. But the scale of this week’s attack shocked even industry veterans. Just as the exploit was unleashed, Taylor Monahan, who’s based in Los Angeles as a researcher at the non-profit security firm, SEAL, was on a group chat with other crypto investigators when someone at blockchain security firm zeroShadow sent a message about strange transactions at Binance. “I’m going to remain optimistic that everything’s fine,” Monahan told herself. But she knew that if things weren’t OK, they were very bad. “It’s like a hack — like, a really big one.” By 4.38pm, Monahan suspected the worst and contacted Tether, the firm that issues the USDT dollar-backed stablecoin. “In our souls, we knew it was a hack,” she said. Tether responded immediately but didn’t acknowledge that there was an infiltration. Less than 30 minutes later, the firm began the process of freezing the transactions on its blockchain, as did Circle, issuer of the USDC stablecoin. Scrolling X

Yi He, Binance’s co-founder and co-chief executive officer, was at home in Abu Dhabi when she first noticed something wrong. The executive had logged off work and was scrolling through X before going to bed about 12.30am in Abu Dhabi (4.30pm in New York). Posts on the social media site alerted her to trouble. Alarmed, she logged back on and saw that Binance’s security and wallet teams – which are empowered to act on hacks without executive sign off – were already at work, trying to stop more losses. Within minutes, the company created a war room that swelled to about 100 people around the world. Yi and hundreds of Binance employees would stay up through the night, co-ordinating efforts within the company and with other crypto firms and law-enforcement agencies including the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the US Secret Service. Natalie Naccache At 5.15pm (New York time), Binance publicly acknowledged it was aware of a “potential security issue” and that it was investigating the rumoured breach.

At 5.18pm, Circle chief executive Jeremy Allaire announced the stablecoin company had frozen more than $US800 million associated with a “potential exploit involving Binance”. Seven minutes later, Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino announced that his firm had frozen more than $US1.5 billion “related to a potential Binance exchange hack”. Related Article Cryptocurrencies Inside a billionaire’s paradise with crypto’s most powerful ex-convict Soon, crypto companies of every stripe started flooding social media to promise onlookers that they were safe. Binance competitors, including Kraken, Coinbase and Bybit, proclaimed they were unharmed. Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs, Chainalysis and Elliptic have all said North Korea is behind the heist. They observed funds stolen from Binance commingle with crypto seized in the Bitget hack, which researchers had already attributed to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. At the weekend, the FBI also blamed North Korea for the hack.

Chainalysis labelled the hack as “the largest in the history of crypto, and one of the single-largest financial crimes of all time”. Still, even as the heist became more widely publicised, hackers continued to drain funds from Binance. The code attackers used gave them access to blockchain accounts owned by Binance and let the hackers empty them, all while exchange funds kept replenishing the accounts. Estimates of the amount stolen crept higher, eventually reaching $US6.3 billion. Mainstream crypto The attack comes at an inopportune time for an industry that is getting unprecedented support from the US government. The Trump administration has been pushing for mainstream adoption of cryptocurrencies and blockchain technology, including through its regulators. In September, the Securities and Exchange Commission approved a rule that allows for public company stocks to trade on blockchains. The Binance hack could undermine those efforts, experts fear. Odysseas Lamtzidis, founder of blockchain security company Phylax Systems, was on a plane travelling to Miami from New York when he saw a Telegram chat discussing the attack. “It was very scary. I remember breathing heavy because it was huge amounts of capital moving around, and people on the plane were asking if I was OK,” he said.

‘It’s still a Wild West.’ Odysseas Lamtzidis, founder of Phylax Systems, He watched as the attackers moved from one wallet to the next, and kept posting on X to alert users. “I think this is very scary for organisations and adoption of crypto because these types of events should be impossible to happen, not improbable,” he said. “It’s still a Wild West.” Binance co-chief executive Richard Teng. Dominic Lorrimer Yi and her co-chief executive, Richard Teng, on Friday confronted the potential reputational damage the attack could do. In a video posted on X, Yi promised Binance would continue to work with law enforcement to find the attackers. The company has vowed to reimburse any users who lost funds in the hack.

“We won’t let the hackers take away the momentum this industry deserves,” she said in her video post, speaking in Mandarin. “Of course, there are areas where we could have done better. We should have invested more in security earlier, and set stricter standards. Going forward, we won’t hold back, whether it’s investing in security or fighting hackers.” On Saturday, the company said it had restored 90 per cent of the tokens which hackers had stolen, pledging to reinstate customers’ ability to withdraw funds the following day. title: Why is James Packer testifying at Benjamin Netanyahu's corruption trial?
text:
IN BRIEF James Packer will testify remotely, rejecting a request from Benjamin Netanyahu's lawyer to travel to Israel.

It's alleged a company linked to Packer has made monthly payments to the law firm representing Netanyahu since 2024.

Australian billionaire James Packer has been called to testify at the corruption trial of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu amid reports of secret payments to a Tel Aviv law firm.

According to reporting by The Sydney Morning Herald, Packer paid at least $1.78 million to Hadad Roth Shenhar, the law firm defending Netanyahu, against claims that he corruptly received benefits from Packer and other wealthy supporters between 2014 and 2016.

It's alleged that for two years, monthly transfers of over $71,000 were wired from an account under Packer's company, Consolidated Press International, to Hadad Roth Shenhar's account.

Consolidated Press International is one of the several private investment arms operated by Packer. It's alleged the first payment was made on 23 September 2024.

If Packer's alleged investments directly or indirectly benefited Netanyahu, the prime minister could face fresh charges.

There is no evidence Netanyahu received any benefit from the payments.

SBS News is not suggesting any wrongdoing by Netanyahu, Packer or Hadad Roth Shenhar.

Packer to testify remotely

Netanyahu's primary defence attorney is Amit Hadad, Hadad Roth Shenhar's most senior lawyer.

On 22 October, Hadad contacted Packer and asked him to travel to Israel to testify at the trial. Hadad also extended the request to Packer's associates Ben Tilley and Guy Jalland.

The Sydney Morning Herald published a segment of Packer's response, written on his behalf by Jalland, who was formerly Consolidated Press Holdings CEO.

Jalland said the trio are not prepared to "travel to Israel for that purpose".

The men said they would testify and agreed to appear remotely via audiovisual link.

Jallad confirmed that he and Tilley had accompanied Packer on "a number of visits to Israel in the period of 2013 to 2016". Neither man is accused of wrongdoing.

It is yet to be determined where Packer will give evidence.

In the letter, Hadad denied Packer's investments are related to Netanyahu's trial — saying Hadad Roth Shenhar represented companies controlled by Packer on other matters.

Packer is yet to comment.

A history of friendship

In February 2018, the Israeli Police named Packer in connection with the bribery and fraud allegations against Netanyahu.

The Australian Federal Police interviewed him as a witness on behalf of their Israeli counterparts the year before.

The Israeli police recommended that the attorney-general indict Netanyahu — who denied all wrongdoing and dismissed rumours that he would resign as prime minister.

READ MORE Netanyahu bloc narrowly ahead as Israeli PM claims Arab parties gained from voter fraud

Packer was linked to Netanyahu's corruption case after allegations that he gifted the politician cigars and champagne sometime between 2014 and 2016.

At the time, Packer and Netanyahu were neighbours, both residing in luxury private villas in Caesarea, on Israel's Mediterranean coast.

However, the pair became estranged in 2016 after the corruption allegations were levelled against Netanyahu.

They were not spotted together again until July 2024, when Packer attended Netanyahu's US Congress address. He would later attend Netanyahu's UN General Assembly address in New York in September the same year.

Australian billionaire James Packer attended Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's speech to the US Congress in July 2024. Source: AFP / Drew Angerer

Packer is the son of the late Australian media mogul Kerry Packer.

The 59-year-old inherited the family fortune after his father passed in 2005 and has a net worth of more than $5.2 billion according to Forbes.

title: 'No area exempt': Nothing off limits as Labor hunts for savings ahead of RBA meeting
text:
In brief Labor has signalled that no area of government spending will be exempt as it searches for budget savings.

Persistent inflation has fuelled expectations that the Reserve Bank will once again raise interest rates.

Nowhere will be off limits for the razor gang while Labor searches for savings as it faces heat for still-rising inflation.

Persistently fast-rising prices have fuelled criticism of high public spending after inflation came in hotter than expected in the year to September.

Accelerating inflation has driven expectations that the Reserve Bank will on Tuesday hike the cash rate to its highest rate in 18 years, pouring more pain on borrowers.

While the Middle East oil shock and ballooning artificial intelligence investment are delivering price pressures largely outside Canberra's control, Labor has also been implored to tighten its belt in December's mid-year budget update.

"I would not say that any area is exempt," Finance Minister Katy Gallagher told ABC's Insiders program on Sunday.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"I'm not saying it's too difficult, but I am saying that there should be some acknowledgement of the world in which we are living and the pressures on the commonwealth budget.

"They are real, they are increasing, and we have to deal with them ... there's a lot of work going into the saving side."

Inflation and government spending

Federal government spending as a percentage of GDP hit 26.9 per cent in the 2025/26 financial year, the highest proportion in four decades outside the COVID-19 pandemic.

The RBA's preferred inflation measure — quarterly trimmed mean — beat the central bank's 0.8 per cent forecast to land at 1 per cent in September.

Headline annual inflation came in at 4.3 per cent, slightly above the consensus estimate.

The result dramatically increased the odds of another interest rate hike on Melbourne Cup day as inflation tracks well outside the RBA's 2-3 per cent target band.

Gallagher described as "overblown" reports of tension between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Treasurer Jim Chalmers over plans the latter had put forward to find budget savings.

On a Nine podcast appearance during the week, the treasurer said he took responsibility for "difficult things in my portfolio", and he would leave it for other ministers to take responsibility for spending on their patches.

Gallagher said Chalmers was simply "putting up his hand for the role that he plays in the decisions around the budget", which was the result of collective cabinet efforts.

While there were "robust discussions" about budget measures, the Labor frontbencher added the treasurer and prime minister had "a very professional and respectful relationship".

"We've all got slightly different jobs and come at things from slightly different perspectives," she said.

Gallagher defends tax breaks, subsidies

The finance minister defended spending on tax breaks for electric vehicles and generous subsidies for home batteries despite the costs of both schemes blowing out amid higher-than-expected demand.

Their uptake by high income-earners has led to suggestions they amount to middle-class welfare, inviting calls for means-testing.

But Gallagher said the same schemes supported other government priorities, such as the renewable energy transition and electrification of the economy.

"Some of the data is showing that this is helping people on the outskirts of cities and in regional areas with some of those cost-of-living pressures and bringing their energy bills down," she said.

Labor has capped the value of EVs eligible for tax breaks and tightened the battery rebate program, but the cost of that scheme has still blown out to $7.2 billion over four years — more than three times its originally forecast cost.

title: Judge dismisses Trump's defamation lawsuit over Epstein birthday letter report
text:
In brief A judge dismissed Trump's lawsuit over a report tied to Jeffrey Epstein.

The ruling kept scrutiny on Trump's past links to the financier.

A US judge on Sunday dismissed President Donald Trump's defamation lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and media magnate Rupert Murdoch over a report that Trump sent a bawdy birthday letter to notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Trump had sued for US$10 billion after the newspaper's story was published in July 2025 detailing the president's alleged 2003 letter to Epstein, which apparently featured a drawing of a naked woman.

Murdoch is the founder of News Corp., which owns the Wall Street Journal.

The report piled scrutiny on Trump from both Democrats and his own Republican party, who rejected the president's attempts to downplay the saga as a hoax and called for a full release of legal files on Epstein.

In Sunday's ruling, Judge Darrin Gayles dismissed Trump's lawsuit with prejudice, meaning Trump cannot file an amended version of the suit, as he did when Gayles turned down an initial version of it back in April.

The judge wrote that in bringing his defamation claim, Trump had both times failed to establish that the defendants "acted with actual malice."

The House Oversight Committee last year published a copy of Trump's alleged birthday note to Epstein, which consists of a short dialogue between "Donald" and "Jeffrey."

"We have certain things in common," says Donald, to which Jeffrey responds: "Yes, we do, come to think of it."

"Enigmas never age, have you noticed that?" asks Donald.

"As a matter of fact, it was clear to me the last time I saw you," says Jeffrey.

"A pal is a wonderful thing. Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret," the note ends, followed by Trump's signature, which takes the place of pubic hair on the nude outline.

Epstein files

Trump's supporters have been obsessed with the Epstein case for years and held as an article of faith that "deep state" elites were protecting a sex ring of Epstein associates, particularly in the Democratic Party and Hollywood.

The president fought for months to prevent the Department of Justice from releasing the so-called "Epstein Files" but eventually signed a law passed by Congress requiring their publication.

Trump's name appears repeatedly in the documents, but he denies any wrongdoing and has not been charged with any criminal offences connected to the affair.

High-profile figures including Britain's former prince Andrew have been publicly disgraced for their associations with Epstein.

Ahead of the 3 November US midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress, Democrats have reportedly spent more than US$35 million on Epstein-related advertisements.

With a Republican majority in the House and Senate, Trump has so far enjoyed relatively little political opposition since taking office in January 2025, giving the courts a key role in limiting him.

In a separate case on Sunday, a new suit was filed to prevent Trump's attempt to erect a huge triumphal arch in front of the iconic military cemetery outside Washington DC.

That is one of a number of projects launched by Trump in a bid to put his personal stamp on the capital, including a ballroom at the White House and a laborious renovation of the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall.

title: The Australian town caught between a housing shortage and rising seas
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

For the past three months, Rebecca Williams has been living in a storage yard without power on the fringes of Far North Queensland.

A broad tarp covers her belongings, and at night she sleeps in a pink swag, which she says offers little shelter from the weather and the noise of trucks hurtling down the nearby highway.

The site also has no toilet.

"None of this is secured, so some nights I feel very unsafe," she tells SBS News.

Her makeshift home sits on the outskirts of Seisia, a small coastal town of around 300 people on the Cape York Peninsula. Rising costs and encroaching seas have created a perfect storm for residents, who are struggling to access affordable and climate-resilient housing.

Williams, 35, is a proud Angkamuthi Seven Rivers woman and works full-time in environmental protection. She says she has been living in "survival mode" for far longer than she’s called the compound home.

She's been waiting for a rental for more than 11 years.

Rebecca Williams is one of around 100 Seisia residents waiting for a long-term rental. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

"I've been told it's based on not having kids. I'm not a priority," she says.

A chronic housing shortage has gripped the community for more than a decade, driven by undersupply, prohibitively high construction costs and overcrowding. Many in the community have no choice but to rely on government-funded housing stock.

While the Queensland Department of Housing is ultimately responsible for social housing across the state, Seisia's local applications are processed by the Northern Peninsula Area Regional Council (NPARC), which also delivers and maintains government-supported homes. But the waitlist is long, forcing some community members to consider leaving their ancestral homeland.

After a decade of couch surfing, living in overcrowded family homes and even taking jobs on boats for two years, Williams moved into her family’s storage yard in June.

The pink swag Rebecca Williams has been sleeping in for the past few months, while awaiting an outcome on her rental application. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

As SBS News was preparing to publish this story, Williams received confirmation from the Department of Housing that it would provide her with emergency accommodation. She expects to move into a government-supported two-bedroom rental with her younger sister in the coming weeks.

She estimates around 100 people in Cape York's Indigenous community are currently waiting for a house — that’s around one in three residents.

"There's a whole heap of us. We're being told to move down to Cairns, but people who are from here, we haven't imagined ourselves living anywhere else," she says.

I see it as structural violence. Maybe a bit of racial, but more structural violence, with not just my generation, but many generations of my family.

A housing crisis on two fronts

Across the Cape York Peninsula, communities like Seisia face similar housing challenges.

As the climate warms and sea levels rise, they are contending with another major threat to their way of life.

Roughly 1,000km north of Cairns, Cape York is bordered by the Coral Sea to the east, the Gulf of Carpentaria to the west and the Torres Strait to the north. Its low-lying, tropical landscape is carved by 21 major river systems, making it home to one of the largest freshwater networks in the country.

Much like the broader Torres Strait region, its topography makes it particularly vulnerable to coastal erosion.

Low-lying coastal areas in Cape York and the surrounding Torres Strait region are at high risk of coastal erosion and flooding events due to climate change. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

It's difficult to predict exactly how much sea-level rise will inundate low-lying areas around the Torres Strait, but the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has identified the region as among the most vulnerable places in the world.

A sea-level rise of just 50cm could make flooding across Australia 300 times more likely, according to the Australian government. By this estimate, a flood that once struck every hundred years would be expected several times a year.

This is a source of deep concern for residents of Cape York, who have witnessed the long-term impacts of flood events and seen First Nations communities displaced.

Sitting on the shores of Seisia Beach, Torres Strait Islander Elders Leonora Adidi and Jenson Warusam recall the "difficult decision" their grandparents made to leave their home in Saibai, a low-lying island in the Torres Strait just a few kilometres off the Papua New Guinea mainland, to establish a new community on the northernmost tip of Australia.

"This was a community that was built by the blood, sweat and tears of our people," Adidi tells SBS News.

Torres Strait Islander Elders Leonora Adidi and Jenson Warusam are among the descendants of the first wave of climate migrants from Saibai. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

The catalyst was a major flooding event, explains Adidi, who is also a linguist and cultural educator from the Suy-Baydham Clan of Bamaga and Saibai.

In 1947, unnatural king tides and heavy monsoon rains struck Saibai, flooding the entire village.

"There wasn't enough fresh water and also fresh food from the gardens to sustain the population," says Adidi, a linguist and cultural educator from the Suy-Baydham Clan of Bamaga and Saibai.

Sabai's chief, Bamaga Ginau, proposed a bold relocation idea.

Source: SBS News

"He put forward his plans that we should all move out and abandon the island," Warusam says.

The community was split: some wanted to leave, while others chose to stay.

Seven families representing seven clan groups sailed south to Cape York in pearl luggers, the M.V. Millard and M.V. Macoy, and established a temporary settlement in the abandoned army camps at Muttee Heads, on Cape York’s west coast. In 1948, the Queensland Government gazetted 44,500 acres (18,008 hectares) as a reserve for Torres Strait Islanders.

More families followed, clearing land and building new houses, until the settlements were renamed Seisia and Bamaga.

This photo, taken in June 1931, shows a dauarti canoe belonging to the Bamaga family, one of the seven Saibai families to migrate permanently to Cape York after 1947. Source: Supplied / Queensland State Archives

"When my grandparents moved here, there was a freak tide, probably due to some underwater event," Adidi says.

In The World's News, a discontinued newspaper formerly published in Sydney, a 1952 headline reads: "Disappearing Island Defies Science", referencing the unnatural tides that inundated Saibai.

But Adidi fears that a one-off event is becoming alarmingly regular.

"It's now getting closer and going into areas where they've never been affected by salt water," she adds.

History repeating itself

While the term climate migration is often associated with people moving from disappearing Pacific islands — such as the recent relocation of Tuvalu citizens to Australia — some historians, climate advocates and members of the Cape York community view Saibai's displaced community as Australia's first internal climate migrants.

Today, the Northern Peninsula Area (NPA) of Cape York remains a gateway to the Torres Strait. Residents are deeply connected to their Saibai roots, sharing the same clan groups, cultural knowledge and totemic systems of the crocodile, or Koedal.

Seisia's Indigenous community was established by Saibai migrants nearly 80 years ago, and many retain strong kinship ties to the island. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

But nearly eight decades after the catastrophic floods that displaced several Saibai families, some NPA residents fear history is repeating itself.

As sea levels rise globally and threaten to submerge the island, Cape York’s chronic housing shortage may not support another generation of migrants from Saibai. Now, both NPARC (the local council) and NPA residents are calling for more government funding to accommodate a future wave of families displaced by rising tides.

Some are taking matters into their own hands.

READ MORE Denis watched his ancestral lands be ravaged as a kid. It sparked a major change

In 2021, two Torres Strait Islander elders, Uncle Pabai Pabai and Uncle Paul Kabai, filed a first-of-its-kind negligence case against the federal government, known as the Australian Climate Case. Kabai, who is based in Saibai, argued the government had failed to protect residents against the threat posed by climate change.

Adidi worked as an interpreter for the Federal Court during the case. The hearings took her back to Saibai for the first time in 25 years.

When Torres Strait Islander Elder Leonora Adidi returned to her ancestral homeland, she witnessed firsthand the damage caused by rising levels. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

"Going on Country and being shown the stark, very drastic changes on Saibai was very shocking. I was in tears," she says.

Her grandmother's garden was unrecognisable. The wide beach she remembered from childhood had been whittled down to a narrow strip. The towering coconut and almond trees had disappeared, replaced by mangroves in the saltwater.

It was like I went to a place I'd never been before.

Scientific evidence heard at the Australian Climate Case suggested that islands such as Saibai, which are only 1.5m above sea level in places, could be unlivable by 2050 if global warming continues on its current trajectory.

"It's going to be underwater if nothing is done, and when that happens, the families have got to move somewhere," Adidi says.

"We established these two communities, Bamaga and Seisia, for our people. In the future, if they want to move, there's always going to be a place for them here."

Pressures on the system

However, the community is already buckling under the demand for new homes. In remote Indigenous communities, government housing can be critical in bridging supply gaps, where private development is extremely limited because remote construction is so expensive.

Former NPARC councillor Frances Elu says more funding is vital to solving the housing crisis in the Northern Peninsula Area. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

Frances Elu, a former NPARC councillor, has witnessed Cape York’s overcrowding crisis unfold over many years.

"[The area has become] overpopulated, I guess — well, I don't guess, I see it. You put more people in an environment that will create a crisis for housing," he says.

But with limited government funding and the need for location-specific infrastructure, there are no simple solutions, he says.

"We've got to somehow assist not only Saibai but Torres Strait Islanders and land is another issue," he says.

There's always room for adapting. At the end of the day, we all related if we're talking about Torres Strait [Islanders].

Although Williams looks set to secure housing now, it took numerous applications over more than a decade. Just before her approval, she had appealed to the NPARC by sending letters and photos documenting her living situation.

She worries for other community members still on the waitlist. Relocation is not an option for many who, like Williams, have deep cultural and kinship ties to the region. Saibai is the Country of her ancestors, and her grandparents were among the first wave of climate-displaced migrants to leave the island for the NPA.

"My grandmother was one of the pioneers coming over looking for fresh water. They've worked really hard building these communities," she says.

She believes the government owes the community "a basic duty of care".

Rebecca Williams may have secured social housing, but many others in her community remain in limbo. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

According to NPARC’s analysis of Census data from 2021, 44 per cent of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in the NPA lacked access to appropriately sized housing, and at least 1,385 additional bedrooms were required to relieve overcrowding. According to the council, this would equate to 462 three-bedroom houses.

NPARC has appealed to the federal government for $137 million to reduce chronic overcrowding. Last month, councillors and NPA community leaders travelled to Canberra to urge the government to fund at least 120 new dwellings across the five NPA communities, as well as maintenance for existing houses.

But building houses in a remote area like Cape York is not easy.

Construction materials and skilled contractors are disproportionately costly. According to NPARC's 2024-2025 budget, 15 new homes cost $15 million to build – roughly $1 million each.

A compounding crisis

For now, both councillors and community members alike are awaiting the federal government’s response.

According to a spokesperson for NPARC, there has been no dedicated federal funding to deliver housing for Queensland Indigenous Communities since 2019.

Council has a role in advocating for investments and to work together with the state government to deliver housing on the ground in our community.

Acknowledging the funding "shortfall", NPARC is calling on the federal government to commit $1 billion from the Housing Australia Future Fund to support Queensland's Indigenous communities.

"Overcrowding has measurable consequences for health and education, including transmission of infectious diseases and acute rheumatic fever," the spokesperson says.

SBS News contacted the Queensland Department of Housing and Public Works for comment but did not receive a response before deadline.

Tess Lea, an anthropologist and Head of Macquarie University’s School of Communication, Society and Culture, says funding social housing is particularly challenging in Indigenous communities.

"The who's responsible question at the moment is kind of everyone and no one. There's no single minister or agency with the responsibility for Indigenous housing," Lea tells SBS News.

"You've got many more Indigenous people dependent on social housing than any other population group in Australia."

While nationally, social housing represents a small minority of total housing stock (in 2025, it accounted for just 4 per cent according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare), much of this problem is structural, Lea explains.

"We've got greater vulnerability [among First Nations communities] just on the basis of the histories of geolocation," she says.

"That's a colonial story – where did water theft start first, where was the most arable land, where was the rich soil."

As sea levels rise, Indigenous communities in and around the Torres Strait are at particular risk of displacement. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

As Indigenous communities have been displaced and forcibly resettled, their vulnerability to climatic and extreme weather events has increased, she explains.

"Australia's at the front lines of climate change," Lea says.

"We're in the age of fire. There's potentially less water or more intense heat events and flooding events."

First Nations communities, she says, are "the collateral … of dragging our feet".

Williams says if another wave of climate migration comes from the Torres Strait islands, she hopes history will not repeat itself, leaving those already displaced from their homelands without access to basic housing.

"We're the people already here, and we're not being looked after," she says.

We're the children of NPA, and we're the homeless children of NPA.

title: What happens when Australia’s inflation basket gets reweighted?
text:
in brief The latest CPI data shows inflation accelerating, with transport, housing and food among key drivers.

The ABS is about to reweight the CPI basket of goods to produce a better measure of inflation.

Last week, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) reported an unexpected spike in inflation in September, prompting fears of more interest rate hikes.

According to the ABS Consumer Price Index (CPI), Australia's annual inflation rate sits at 4.3 per cent — up from 4 per cent in August.

Amongst the largest contributors to rising inflation were housing, which rose 5.2 per cent; alcohol and tobacco, which rose 4.3 per cent and health, which rose 3.7 per cent.

The ABS will be reweighting the CPI basket of goods in January to better reflect current spending trends and produce a more accurate CPI, a crucial exercise as Australians adjust their spending amid continued rising costs.

According to retail expert at the University of Sydney Business School, Lisa Asher, a reweighting exercise is undertaken to "adequately reflect" what people are "actually spending" their money on.

While a change usually occurs at the end of each year, the ABS had postponed the 2026 change to January. The last reweight was in late 2025.

"Some of the key changes or movements that we saw last year and this year focus much more on the increase in food and non-alcoholic beverages, as a larger percentage, as well as health costs and transport," Asher said.

While the ABS does not flag early what the new weightings may look like, previous changes offer some clues.

In 2025, the biggest weighting increases were in education, health and food and non-alcoholic beverages and the larger weight decreases were in furnishings, household equipment and services, alcohol and tobacco and housing.

What is the CPI and how is calculated?

The CPI is "really a measure of inflation" or "price changes in the economy" and it is based on a representative basket of goods and services for Australian households, head of price statistics at the ABS, Rachael McCririck, said.

The CPI provides a "sense of the underlying price pressures in the economy" but isn't a good measure for how the cost of living crisis is impacting individual households.

"The CPI is really an aggregate measure that informs policymakers and decision-makers about aggregate trends, it informs things like monetary and fiscal policy settings," she said.

"When we talk about the cost of living, we're really talking about an individual household and what pressures they're facing in their day-to-day lives — so to get a sense of that you have to look at the individual consumption basket."

To calculate the CPI, the ABS collects prices for items grouped into 87 categories and 11 groups. Every month, the ABS calculates the price changes of each item from the previous month and aggregates them to work out the inflation rate for the basket.

Prices are collected from a variety of retailers across the eight capital cities and the ABS uses methods like web-scraping and online and telephone interviews with retailers.

A knitter and an EV owner, McCririck said her basket would differ from the "average household's basket".

"But the weights that we give to the basket for the CPI are based on the average household experience," she said.

How are CPI items and weights chosen?

In deciding which goods and services to include in the CPI basket and what their weights should be, the ABS uses data about how much – and on what – households in Australia spend their income.

If households spend more of their income on one item, that item will have a larger weight in the CPI.

McCririck said reweights are based on the ABS' household expenditure survey.

"We've grown forward the CPI weights by looking ... at how trends in the household expenditure change — we've grown the weight forward each year manually," she said.

Looking at the reweight in 2025, the weight for alcohol and tobacco fell because sales of legal tobacco had fallen as smoking rates decline, although it did not include vapes and illicit tobacco.

The weight for housing also fell because home buying declined amid a shortage in new construction and supply. Dwelling commencements in 2024 were the lowest in over ten years.

In 2024, school fees rose in 2024 and there were more non-government school enrolments forcing the weight for education to go up for 2025.

Due to the rise in airfares, Australian household spending on overseas holidays rose so the weight for international holiday travel and accommodation increased.

Inflationary pressures are 'going to persist'

Regardless of the weights, Asher told SBS News that rising inflation is a trend that is likely to continue.

"The wars will continue, which means that fuel prices will continue to be high and that has a flow-on effect on goods, logistics and transport systems — which flows onto anything that's imported," she said.

"Many materials, even if they are locally produced here, will increase."

She said inflationary pressures have seen Australians reduce their spending — a habit she hopes can continue into the Christmas period.

"As we move into the Christmas period, people are worse off now than they were at the beginning of the year with inflation — wage growth hasn't kept up," Asher said.

"Some people will be inclined to still spend at Christmas because they feel obliged to do so. I really think that people should be okay to pull back and not overdo it or put things on credit.

"As we move into next year, it's still going to be incredibly tough. Many of the challenges we're seeing are going to persist."

title: As the world grows more divided, Canada and Europe are betting on each other
text:
In brief The EU and Canada announced a new alliance as both faced growing pressure from the United States.

The agreement deepened cooperation on Ukraine, trade, critical minerals and AI.

The EU and Canada announced an alliance on Saturday, aimed at cementing their own relations in the face of US President Donald Trump's moves to tear up US ties with its old partners.

Canada agreed to contribute to a 90-billion-euro ($142.3 billion) support loan for Ukraine and work more closely with the EU on anything from critical minerals to artificial intelligence, after a two-day summit in Montreal.

"The world's becoming more dangerous and divided. Our societies are being shaken by new storms," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told a press conference, mentioning eroding democratic norms and "the weaponisation of trade."

"Together, Canada and the European Union are anchoring the ground. Anchoring our ground to uphold our values while forming a protective canopy under which our citizens can all thrive," he said after talks with EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa.

Already sharing a free trade agreement, Canada and the EU have sought to move closer together since Trump's shock return to power.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Both Canada and the EU have been hit with US tariffs and territorial threats.

In Montreal, they sketched out a two-tier partnership that von der Leyen, the European Commission president, stressed was "not against anyone else, but for our common strength."

But the plan was partially overshadowed by an intra-EU squabble over what the new relationship should be called, which led to some mixed messaging at the summit.

Unable to fully join the bloc, Canada would become its first "associate member," von der Leyen, said, doubling down on a term opposed by Germany and a handful of other EU states.

The group had successfully pushed to have the label dropped from a joint summit statement, arguing it doesn't exist in EU treaties and needed defining.

Von der Leyen was, however, backed by Carney who also used the title as he addressed journalists after the talks, adding its "substance" would be determined in the coming months.

From the EU's point of view, the term defines the unique partnership the EU has with Canada and entails aligning policies, such as on climate and artificial intelligence, Canada joining some EU programs, and creating a stable governance framework.

Broader alliance

As part of this, Canada will have a more stable presence at the EU table.

Carney will take part in an EU leaders summit in June, and European commissioners and Canadian ministers would hold a separate meeting in the spring, Costa, the European Council president, said.

More broadly, Canada and the EU would form the "nucleus" of a larger "alliance for the future" open to other partners, von der Leyen said.

This "will focus on increasing our collective sovereignty and resilience in areas such as AI, energy, critical minerals, quantum, and beyond," Carney said.

A senior EU official explained a key part of it would be coordinating economic security measures, like tariffs, so that they do not inadvertently harm members of the group.

To kick off work, the EU and Canada signed a digital trade deal and a separate pact allowing the European Investment Bank to back Canadian critical mineral projects.

READ MORE EU proposes landmark associate membership for Canada

Canada is rich in rare earths and critical minerals that Europe currently sources mostly from China, but needs massive infrastructure investment to jump-start its mining industry.

The allies agreed to deepen cooperation on satellite connectivity and navigation and artificial intelligence — a field where they are playing catch-up with the US and China.

They also launched work towards Canada's participation in EU initiatives like the Erasmus program, which allows university students to spend a semester abroad, and the Galileo satellite program — an alternative to the American Global Positioning System (GPS).

Europe opened its supercomputing infrastructure to Canadian researchers, industry and start-ups.

Finally, Carney said Canada will join the EU's 90-billion-euro support loan for Ukraine with an initial participation of 500 million euros, in what von der Leyen described as "a powerful message" of support to Ukraine.

The EU has been looking for help to plug gaps in Ukraine's finances, as Russia's war of invasion grinds on.

title: King Charles has expressed sorrow for slavery. Why won't he apologise?
text:
In brief King Charles stopped short of apologising for Britain's role in slavery ahead of a key summit.

Caribbean leaders have prepared to renew their push for reparations and action.

King Charles has, since 2022, expressed sorrow for the suffering caused by slavery without crossing a line that Britain has long resisted: an apology.

That balancing act is likely to be tested at next week's Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda, where Caribbean leaders who back a reparations campaign through the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) are expected to press their case.

Buckingham Palace has indicated Charles would not apologise on behalf of Britain, which has repeatedly ruled out financial reparations over its role in the transatlantic slave trade.

Speaking in the Bahamas on Tuesday ahead of a Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting that begins on Sunday, Charles said it was "only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past." He said leaders from affected countries would discuss the issue at the summit.

But Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, chair of the Bahamas' National Reparations Committee, said that did not go far enough. "We do not need more carefully crafted words about healing," she said in a statement. "We need action equal with the scale of the harm inflicted."

On Friday, about 15 people protested ahead of the king's arrival in Georgetown, Guyana. They gathered outside the Umana Yana, a conical palm-thatched hut originally built for the 1972 Non-Aligned Foreign Ministers Conference, where Charles later delivered a speech.

"It's an opportunity to try to impress upon him this historic responsibility for what took place here," said Terence Campbell, a member of parliament for the opposition APNU, who stood among the protesters holding a banner that read: "No apology will return what was stolen. Reparations now!"

Royal links to slavery under scrutiny

From the 15th to the 19th century, at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery by European traders, with Britain transporting an estimated 3.2 million people across the Atlantic, making it one of the biggest slave-trading nations, according to the Transatlantic Slave Trade Database.

Alan Lester, a University of Sussex historian whose research spans the legacies of slavery and empire, said opponents of the reparations movement had "successfully weaponised" the idea that reparations simply meant writing a cheque, an idea that few Western governments will countenance.

Instead, Caribbean leaders often frame their demands in terms of debt relief, development finance, education, healthcare and climate resilience, measures they say would address inequalities rooted in slavery and colonialism.

"I think King Charles III is in a difficult position because you can express sorrow about something, but an apology goes much further," royal commentator Afua Hagan said.

Buckingham Palace said in 2023 that Charles had given his support to research that was examining the monarchy's links to slavery after the Guardian newspaper reported on a document showing a historical connection.

In a more recent finding, independent researcher Desiree Baptiste told Reuters her forthcoming book, "George IV, Empire, and Objects of Prestige," would cite House of Lords papers and other British government records showing that profits derived from enslaved labour helped fund furniture and decorative work commissioned by George IV at royal residences.

In a response, the Royal Collection Trust, a charity that maintains and displays artworks and historic objects held in trust by the king, said constant research helped it to keep its records "continually under review in order to improve the information presented on an object or subject".

title: 'A complex attack': What we know about the largest crypto heist in history
text:
In brief Binance said it was working to contain what may be the biggest crypto theft on record.

Investigators linked the multibillion-dollar hack to a group tied to North Korea.

Cryptocurrency platform Binance said on Saturday it was working to resolve a "complex attack" that affected around US$6.3 billion ($8.9 billion) in funds, in what is thought to be the biggest ever crypto heist, with investigators pointing to hackers linked to North Korea.

Blockchain investigation firm TRM Labs said it had "high confidence" that the attack was orchestrated by a North Korea-affiliated group called TraderTraitor, the same group blamed for the US$1.5 billion ($2.1 billion) theft from the Bybit platform in February last year.

Another analytics firm, Elliptic, also attributed the attack to North Korea-linked hackers, according to industry outlet CoinDesk.

TraderTraitor is believed to be part of Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for the Seth Rogen comedy film The Interview, which mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes, said investigations had "uncovered additional points of breach," contrary to initial findings that suggested the hack involved a single compromised laptop.

"This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it," Binance wrote on X.

The company confirmed on its X account for Latin America that "the total estimated impact is around US$6.3 billion," four times the amount taken in the Bybit hack, the biggest cyberattack of its kind until now.

Binance warned the figure "may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets."

It said around US$3 billion ($4.2 billion) in affected assets had been frozen.

Customers’ account balances have not been touched, but they cannot move funds off the platform while withdrawals remain suspended.

Binance initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals but later said deposits were unaffected. At about 0900 GMT Friday, it said it was on track to resume withdrawals in 45 hours.

READ MORE Time for a trip to New Zealand? Why Australian travellers now have an advantage

Fund freeze

The company had said on X that initial investigation suggested the hack involved a compromised laptop belonging to a "DevOps engineer," allowing the unauthorised party to execute unauthorised withdrawal transactions.

"We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets," it said, promising to share a detailed technical analysis once investigations were complete.

The unauthorised withdrawals drained Binance's hot wallets — the online wallets the exchange uses to process customer transfers — across several blockchains, according to CoinDesk.

Binance earlier posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages, insisting that "user funds are completely safe" but also saying it would "cover all losses."

Paolo Ardoino, the boss of Tether, a company that issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT, said his firm froze about US$1.6 billion ($2.2 billion) "related to a potential Binance exchange hack."

Jeremy Allaire, who runs cryptocurrency platform Circle, said his company had frozen more than US$800 million ($1.1 billion) in USDC.

USDT and USDC are both "stablecoins," or digital currencies whose value is linked to a traditional currency, the US dollar.

The US Department of Justice and the FBI did not respond to requests for comment.

Crypto prices tumble

For several hours before Binance confirmed the attack, industry observers said hackers had managed to reach the platform.

The prices of most major cryptocurrencies fell on news of the cyberattack, except for the stablecoins, which by definition can only fluctuate within tight margins.

Bitcoin plunged nearly five per cent after the news, falling overnight to around US$76,400 ($108,600), its lowest level since mid-September, before recovering slightly to trade at about US$77,300 ($109,800).

Ethereum dropped nearly six per cent, while BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10 per cent.

The attack on Binance comes as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

title: Time for a trip to New Zealand? Why Australian travellers now have an advantage
text:
While the prospect of higher interest rates could leave borrowers with less money to spend, it has come as good news for the Australian dollar.

The Aussie surged above NZ$1.25 this week for the first time in more than 13 years, making holidays across the Tasman more affordable for Australians.

Our currency has gained more than 10 per cent against the New Zealand dollar over the past year, giving Australian travellers greater purchasing power.

Two contrasting economic developments helped drive the latest move.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Wednesday's stronger-than-expected inflation report pushed the market-implied probability of a Melbourne Cup Day interest rate rise by the Reserve Bank of Australia above 80 per cent, supporting the Australian dollar.

Across the Tasman, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised markets by leaving interest rates on hold.

Like Australia, New Zealand is also grappling with inflation above its central bank's target, with annual consumer prices rising 3.7 per cent.

Differences in interest rate expectations between the two countries have helped push the Australian dollar higher, potentially making a New Zealand getaway better value.

Major discounts coming for Australian shoppers

Bigger discounts could be on the way during Black Friday and the Christmas period as many Australian retailers battle for shoppers amid slow sales growth.

The sluggish growth in sales could be a sign that consumers are holding back from spending big during the sales, or that cost of living pressures and the prospect of higher interest rates are weighing on household budgets.

Woolworths CEO Amanda Bardwell told shareholders at the company's annual general meeting (AGM) this week that four in 10 Australians say they often struggle to make ends meet. The supermarket giant estimates groceries account for 10 per cent of household spending among borrowers.

But that hasn't stopped Woolworths from making what its CEO described as a good start to the financial year, with food sales rising nearly 7 per cent in the three months to September. It's doing better than Coles, which reported slower sales growth over the same period at 3.6 per cent, still topping $10 billion in revenue.

It seems that even in tough times, people have to eat — who would have thought?

Betashares investment strategist Hugh Lam told the SBS On the Money podcast that shares in the consumer staples sector have risen about 20 per cent so far this year.

"A lot of companies within there, like Woollies, Coles and even Bega Cheese, are benefiting because these are sectors of the market where people are still going to be spending despite where we are in the economic cycle," Lam said.

For retailers selling more discretionary items, however, the picture isn't as rosy.

This week, Super Retail Group, which owns Rebel, Supercheap Auto, BCF and Macpac, said weaker consumer confidence and pressure on discretionary spending had weighed on its business.

It specifically pointed to higher petrol prices as a factor behind the decline in quarterly like-for-like sales at outdoor retailers BCF and Macpac.

JB Hi-Fi, which also operates The Good Guys and kitchen and bathroom retailer e&s, reported negative comparable sales growth across its Australian businesses.

It highlights the pressures many businesses in the discretionary sector — selling wants rather than needs — are facing in this economic climate.

"I think what this means … is potential discounting from these retailers which is of course going to hit margins," Lam said.

"And that's because higher interest rates mean that there's less discretionary money everyday Australians can spend on."

Even Bunnings, owned by Wesfarmers, has seen sales growth moderate, according to Wesfarmers CEO Rob Scott at the company's AGM.

But he said the group's Kmart business was performing well as shoppers increasingly sought value.

For consumers, that could mean more bargains during Black Friday and Christmas sales, as retailers compete harder for every dollar.

Will you have to pay for Claude and its competitors?

AI chatbot Claude's owner, Anthropic, lodged its prospectus this week as it prepares to list on the US sharemarket.

The filing offered investors a detailed look at the company's extraordinary revenue growth, mounting expenses and the risks associated with developing increasingly powerful artificial intelligence.

Among the most serious risks identified were "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such (AI) systems were misused, replicated, weaponized [sic], or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".

Loftus Peak chief investment officer Alex Pollack told the SBS On the Money podcast that other potentially catastrophic threats already exist, including nuclear and cyber risks.

"But the question you’ve got to ask yourself is, what is the probability of those risks happening?" Pollack said.

But buried among the warnings was another risk with more immediate implications for the millions of people using AI chatbots for free.

Anthropic warned that its marketing strategies, including free trials and free subscription tiers, might fail to deliver sufficient financial benefits.

READ MORE A $3 billion downgrade could send a ripple through a surging Australian industry

"If the costs of supporting free users exceed the value we derive from their eventual conversion or other benefits such as network effects and word-of-mouth referrals, our business, financial condition and results of operations could be adversely affected."

Could that eventually mean an end to free access?

The prospectus doesn't suggest Anthropic has made such a decision, but it does highlight the financial challenge of offering expensive AI services at no cost.

Anthropic reported revenue of US$16.28 billion ($23.12 billion) in the six months to the end of June 2026, compared with US$1.16 billion ($1.65 billion) in the same period a year earlier.

But that extraordinary growth comes with enormous costs.

The company spent nearly US$9 billion ($12.78 billion) on computing and infrastructure over those six months, accounting for more than half its total operating expenses.

It's a reminder that while AI chatbots might be free for many people today, the technology powering them is anything but cheap.

title: 'Pauline is jumping at shadows': Labor denies it tried to lure One Nation MP David Farley
text:
In brief Labor has insisted there's nothing "unusual" about offering David Farley additional staff, citing his Farrer electorate's size.

Pauline Hanson says One Nation is concerned the government is trying to "exert undue political influence over politicians".

Labor insists it is not trying to woo rookie MP David Farley into defecting from One Nation after offering him a much-prized and highly paid extra staffer.

The offer came hand-delivered to the Farrer MP's Parliament House office on Monday but was rejected by One Nation leader Pauline Hanson over accusations it amounted to a bribe.

"These actions have left David and One Nation deeply concerned that the government is seeking to use taxpayer funds to exert undue political influence over politicians," Hanson said in a statement on Thursday.

The offer comes as the Labor government seeks to fight off a surge in the polls by the populist One Nation, which has also eaten into the voting base of the right-leaning Coalition.

Farley has never publicly ruled out moving to Labor and once even tried to stand as a candidate for the party in 2021, having once also been a member of the Nationals.
