An upsizing couple paid $2.14 million for a renovated Alexandria terrace with a rooftop garden at auction on Saturday, beating two others and still securing a discount to the reserve. The three-bedroom home at 182 Henderson Road had a kitchen and dining area that led out to a courtyard and then a smart rooftop terrace for entertaining, set above the garage. The property was one of 985 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 48 per cent from 564 reported results throughout the week, while 208 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. The clearance rate has edged up from the low it reached last week, when the preliminary result was 45 per cent, its lowest all year. But it remains far below the 60 per cent threshold that indicates a market balanced between buyers and sellers, and suggests prices are still falling.

Advertisement

The Alexandria home was offered with a price guide of $2 million and drew three registered bidders at auction, all of whom participated. Related Article Auctions Inner-city warehouse apartment sells for $150,000 below reserve Bidding began at $2 million and two parties pushed the price to $2.1 million, when a third buyer jumped in. The home sold for $2.14 million. The reserve price had been $2.25 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide.

“The owners did the renovation – did a beautiful job adding this Mediterranean courtyard,” Ray White Erskineville/Alexandria/Glebe/Surry Hills selling agent Shaun Stoker said. “That was what really stood out to buyers, was this beautiful rooftop garden above the garage.” He added that the vendors had since moved to Brisbane for work and decided to sell their Sydney home. The buyers are a young couple from Redfern upsizing from a unit who like the lock-up garage, a rare feature in the neighbourhood, Stoker said, adding they also like the area and its proximity to transport options.

The other two buyers were first-home hopefuls. Related Article Title Deeds John Paul Young sold a $266k Bronte home. It just resold for $12m Speaking broadly about the market, he said there are buyers looking, but showing interest only if they see value. “We are getting a good number of groups coming through opens, it just seems a lot of buyers are on the sidelines just waiting,” he said. “The numbers out there is just as good as in a good market – just they are sitting waiting.”

In Surry Hills, a syndicate of investors learning about the renovation process sold a stylish two-bedroom apartment in a full brick building for $1,338,000. The renovated home at 2/9-19 Nickson Street featured natural stone and marble details, banquette seating in the dining room and access to a communal rooftop area. Four parties registered for the home, listed with a price guide of $1.25 million, and all four participated. Bidding began at $1.15 million and was a little slow at the start as buyers hesitated. It sold for a little under the reserve of $1,345,000.

The winner was a woman from Sydney’s north who intends for her daughter to live there, said Ray White Touma Taylor selling agent Con Fotaras. Related Article Property market How much more house sellers can make by going to auction The home last sold for $1,065,000 in December last year. Bernadette Janson, of The School of Renovating, managed a unit trust of 19 female investors with a minimum $50,000 buy-in, who made updates including to the kitchen and bathroom as well as fresh paint. The project splits profits after paying for debt and costs. Fotaras praised Janson’s work. “She nailed the renovation. It was a really good renovation, the response was really good,” he said.” He added that there were few homes for sale in the area as the market has come back a little.

“You can wait for a better deal but you might not get a better property.” On the northern beaches, a renovated duplex in Curl Curl sold for $1.82 million at auction, surpassing its guide price and reserve. The two-bedroom home at 1/68 Adams Street was close to Curl Curl Beach and came with a stone-topped kitchen in a stylish shade of avocado. Proceedings began at $1.65 million and two of the three registered bidders, all young locals, pushed the price higher in rapid-fire bids of mostly $10,000. The price rose above the guide of $1.7 million and the reserve of $1.8 million.

The winner is a young man from the local area. The vendors are also locals, selling their investment property, Cunninghams Real Estate selling agent Anita Wildash said. She said the home stood out because it was near the beach and fully renovated, but this was not the only home that has sold for more than its guide price lately. “It is all about pricing the property right and in this market we are working hard to do that,” she said.

A public secondary school in Melbourne’s south-east has won the approval of parents, defying a trend for those on the city’s fringe to record lower parental satisfaction scores due to ageing facilities and student bullying. An analysis of the annual opt-in survey of more than 300 government-run secondary schools across the state, found Stonnington had the most satisfied parents – giving the schools an average rating of 89.2 per cent. Average satisfaction scores are similarly high for schools in Glen Eira (85 per cent) and Port Phillip (82.6 per cent). By contrast, Cardinia (55.8 per cent), Nillumbik (59.1 per cent) and Melton (61.5 per cent) were on average home to the Melbourne schools with the least satisfied parents with in 2025. While schools in growth corridors tended to have lower scores, the area of Casey rose above. The average parental satisfaction of schools there is 72.9 per cent, driven up by select-entry Nossal High School (96.3) and Cranbourne West Secondary College (97.6 per cent).

Advertisement

Still, experts say the figures highlight the stress public schools in growth areas are under, and the need to ensure government funding and services back up the commitment of teachers. National Growth Areas chief executive Bronwen Clark said communities on the city’s fringe were grappling with a number of pressures as the population expanded. “I think that all plays into a catching-up process, that organic growth of transport systems, school growth, maturity in the school community takes time,” she said. “It may well be that part of the frustration for parents is the transport to get their kids to school, and the traffic and the congestion. And it may well be that some secondary schools have a vast number of portable classrooms.” Statewide, schools that ran from prep to year 12 were ranked lower (70.1 per cent) than standalone secondary schools (74.1 per cent), with P-12 schools more commonly located in regional areas with lower satisfaction levels.

Advertisement

Regionally, parents gave the most positive ratings to schools in Pyrenees Shire (93.8 per cent), and the lowest in Wodonga (48.2 per cent). Closer to the city centre, parents rated two Melbourne schools with scores of 100 per cent satisfaction: Box Hill Senior Secondary College, in Melbourne’s east, which has 282 students, and Bindjiroo Yaluk Community School, which has just 79 students across campuses in Richmond and Coburg. Cranbourne West Secondary College principal Rob Duncan (back middle) with his 2025 VCE high achievers. Joe Armao Cranbourne West Secondary College principal Rob Duncan said the Casey area school’s high parental satisfaction correlated with other strong results, across VCE scores, student engagement and strong management of bullying.

Advertisement

“Because we’re a reasonably multicultural community, we obviously try to make sure we’ve got staff who the parents feel that they can communicate with,” Duncan said, adding teachers spoke several different languages. “We make ourselves as accessible as possible when parents have concerns, that’s the entire leadership team. And we have a genuine focus on positive outcomes for kids.” Parents Victoria chief executive Gail McHardy said that while families could face different educational experiences depending on where they lived, survey results should be used as a starting point and “not a definitive verdict on a school or its staff”. Related Article Education The Melbourne schools with the most portable buildings and the impact on students “Parental satisfaction reflects many factors: the quality of relationships between schools and families, student learning, safety, bullying, mental health and wellbeing, disability inclusion, teacher availability, facilities and access to specialist support … But every school is different, and we should not assume geography alone explains the results,” she said.

Advertisement

“Parents in growth corridors may be navigating additional pressures around school capacity, infrastructure and access to support services. These are system-planning issues, not a reflection of the commitment of local school communities.” In Cardinia Shire, the average school’s parent satisfaction result was 55.8 per cent, the lowest across metropolitan areas. Parents at one local secondary school told The Age that while they were happy with the school’s teachers and buildings (which recently received $11.3 million for upgrades and modernisation), they were concerned about bullying and student suspensions. “I’ve found the teachers have been really good,” said Jayde Valsveld, who attended the school herself and has sent four children there. “If there’s been any issues, they’ve been involved. And now with all the new buildings going in, they’re way overdue.” Though parents reported some students being suspended multiple times without a change in behaviour, Valsveld said: “With every school, the bullying could be improved; the way bullies are handled discipline-wise.”

Advertisement

A spokesperson for the Department of Education said the school treated all allegations of bullying seriously and addressed incidents with appropriate and proportionate consequences. I still don’t Since 2024, every government school parent has had the opportunity to complete the survey. “Parent satisfaction has continued to improve in recent years, alongside student perceptions,” the department’s spokesperson said. “Education works best when schools and families are working in partnership, and parent surveys and forums are just some of the tools used to cultivate that approach.”

The organisers of Australia’s biggest triathlon have been forced to cancel the swim leg of the race for the first time in the event’s history after multiple shark sightings over the weekend. The Noosa Triathlon is the largest Olympic-distance triathlon event in the world, drawing more than 13,000 competitors to the Sunshine Coast town over the five-day festival. In an update posted to the event’s Instagram, organisers warned Sunday’s swim course would be altered “due to marine life sightings” which closed Noosa’s Main Beach for periods on Saturday. The Noosa Triathlon usually begins with a 1500-metre swim off Noosa’s Main Beach. They hoped an “M-shaped” swim bringing athletes closer to the shore would allay safety concerns, but an updated post published Sunday morning stated “due to marine life present … the swim will not be taking place”.

Advertisement

Noosa Triathlon spokesman Craig Heydon said the decision was made to cancel the swim altogether as there had been a number of shark sightings over the last few weeks and days, with some animals sighted within the race’s swim perimeter. “[The race has] a 1.5 kilometre swim, which goes a couple of 100 metres offshore, and the animals [sighted] were within that space,” Heydon explained. “So the decision was made that it wasn’t safe to put swimmers in the water today.” This is the first time the swim leg has been cancelled in the event’s 43-year history.

Advertisement

“We obviously had quite a lot of rain in recent weeks, which might have been part of what led to having them in the water,” he said. “But from an event perspective, the team was able to pivot really quickly, and our athletes are still out on course now and having a great day.” Competitors in the event’s elite race started at 6.15 am on Sunday, swapping the 1500-metre swim with a five-kilometre run, followed by a 40-kilometre ride and a 10-kilometre run. Related Article Olympics How much will it cost getting to Brisbane 2032? A legend’s daughter and Olympic hopeful reveals For the age group athletes who make up the majority of the race, the swim component was swapped for a short beach run.

Advertisement

“[Athletes] put a lot of training into these events, so they would have liked to be able to do a triathlon,” Heydon said. “But they’re certainly very understanding of the reasons why the decision was made today.” Despite the disruptions, Australian triathlete Matt Hauser defended his Noosa Triathlon title, claiming victory on Sunday with a one hour, 39 minutes and 34 second finish. Australia’s Matthew Hauser competes during the men’s individual triathlon competition at the 2024 Summer Olympics, AP “You have to keep adapting to situations and changes, and we had to make of it what we could and the crowd got a kick out of it,” Hauser said of the 45-minute notice of the race changes.

“It’s Noosa, you have to do the race justice and give it a crack.“ Fellow Paris Olympian Luke Willian finished in second place (1:42:59), followed by US racer John Reed. Fellow Paris Olympian Natalie Van Coevorden claimed the women’s title, surprising herself in what was her first race over the distance since the 2024 event. With AAP

Exclusive TechnologySpace Europe’s answer to Elon Musk’s Starlink wants to build satellites in Australia David Swan November 1, 2026 — 1:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Helsinki: A Finnish satellite maker says it could help Australia build its own alternative to Elon Musk’s Starlink, made locally and owned by Australians. ReOrbit, which assembles communications satellites for defence customers inside a former Ford car factory in Helsinki, wants to set up manufacturing in Australia with local companies and the government. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carrying 53 Starlink satellites. (Craig Bailey/Florida Today via AP) AP “I’m very interested personally, making this happen in Australia,” chief commercial officer Markus Räikkönen told this masthead in an interview. He plans to visit in February. The pitch arrives as Australia leans harder on satellites it does not control. From next year, the Universal Outdoor Mobile Obligation requires the mobile carriers to provide basic outdoor voice and text coverage through a low-earth-orbit satellite partner, so a phone with no tower in range can still send a message.

Advertisement

ReOrbit chief commercial officer Markus Räikkönen. The Australian Telecommunications Alliance, the industry’s peak body, says that market “does not currently provide any competitive options”. Telstra and Optus have both signed with Elon Musk’s Starlink for satellite-to-phone services. In late October, Musk said SpaceX had restricted Ukraine’s Starlink service, accusing its military of breaching the terms by using it for “offensive drone strikes”, which Ukrainian officials dispute. Ukraine says the problems hampered its defensive operations for more than a week. Musk had earlier denied deliberately throttling the service, which was restored after US President Donald Trump said he had told Musk to “put it back”. Räikkönen said it matters little to someone shopping online whose satellite carries the signal. For defence, he said, it is “extremely important who controls the satellite connectivity”. “Can somebody turn it off? Can somebody slow it down?” Sovereignty used to mean leasing a reserved slice of capacity on another operator’s satellite, he said. Governments now want the whole system. “I want to own my satellites, my ground station. I want to operate the satellite,” he said, describing what customers ask for, with data landing in their own country and “no restrictions or kill switch” outside it.

Advertisement

Australia would need more of them than most. Finland could cover its critical communications with a single geostationary satellite, which sits fixed about 36,000 kilometres above the equator, Räikkönen said. “For Australia it’s a massive land area,” he said, and several would be needed. Elon Musk’s Starlink has agreements with both Telstra and Optus. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson A sovereign version of Starlink, using satellites about 550 kilometres up, would need a constellation of about 600 to 1000 satellites for Australia, he said, though a service could start with fewer. ReOrbit would act as the systems integrator and hand over the know-how, he said. “With a company like ReOrbit we could actually do it in Australia and everything could be owned by locals,” he said. One of ReOrbit’s satellites.

Advertisement

Australia has tried this before. In 2024, the Defence Department cancelled JP9102, a $6.9 billion sovereign military satellite communications system built around new geostationary satellites, a year and a half after awarding the contract to Lockheed Martin Australia. ReOrbit was founded in 2019 and has about 160 staff, adding more than 10 a month, Räikkönen said. Its biggest investors are Finnish pension funds, including Varma and Elo. That helps in defence sales, Räikkönen said, because governments wary of choosing between American and Chinese suppliers can buy Finnish without upsetting anyone. “If you buy from Finland, nobody cares.” Related Article Opinion

Aviation Starlink’s growing influence has one big point of failure Chris Zappone Senior reporter, aviation Chief executive Sethu Saveda Suvanam has pitched ReOrbit as an affordable alternative to Starlink for countries that cannot build their own satellites, TechCrunch reported when the company raised €45 million ($71.7 million) last year, in what the site described as a record round for a European space start-up. He said it had signed a contract worth “some hundreds of millions” with one country and memorandums of understanding with others. ReOrbit’s first satellite, which runs artificial intelligence on board to analyse images before sending them down, is due to launch in February on a SpaceX rideshare flight. Räikkönen said whether SpaceX keeps launching rivals’ satellites is “completely on them to decide”, though he expects it to, because the business helps pay for its rockets. The launch is set for the same month as his Australian trip.

title: The prime slice of coastal Sydney with roads, paths – and almost no homes
text:
Advertisement

NationalNSWCity life The prime slice of coastal Sydney with roads, paths – and almost no homes David Barwell November 1, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. When plans were first unveiled to develop a prime stretch of coastal land in Sydney’s south-east into hundreds of new homes, confidence appeared high, as construction crews got to work building all the roads, footpaths and residential lots in preparation for an influx of new residents. But more than a decade later, only a handful of homes have been completed, the footpaths are largely empty, and the streets are frequented mainly by the occasional street sweeper, cyclist and parents taking their teenage children for supervised learner driver lessons. An aerial view of the Little Bay site. Sam Mooy Amid debate over new housing in Sydney’s eastern suburbs, the site’s owner and Australia’s richest property developer, Harry Triguboff, is embarking on a new plan to develop the land after three previous proposals to build thousands of apartments failed to gain planning approval and faced strong community opposition. Through his company, Meriton, Triguboff has submitted a new proposal for 505 homes in buildings of up to five storeys on the coastal site overlooking Little Bay Beach and the fairways of The Coast Golf Club.

Advertisement

The plan, which includes an initial stage of 100 homes, three of which would be affordable dwellings, received initial support this month from the NSW government’s Housing Delivery Authority, a planning body established to boost housing supply through streamlined assessments that bypass local councils. Related Article Development ‘Like some sort of giant, concrete zombie’: Meriton makes new bid for redevelopment of Little Bay The proposal marks a significant departure from the scale of Meriton’s previous plans, which included an application for 1900 apartments rejected by the Sydney Eastern City Planning Panel in 2021, a rezoning bid for 1600 homes in 2023 and an application for 2600 apartments across two 27-storey towers last year. Instead, the latest proposal brings the development closer to the scale of an approved masterplan Meriton inherited when it acquired the site for $245 million in 2017, which permitted up to 450 homes in buildings of up to five storeys. While Meriton declined to comment on its latest proposal, the company has consistently maintained its commitment to developing the site.

Advertisement

The change in scale has been cautiously welcomed by some residents including Olde Lorenzen, a founding member of community group Save Little Bay which has spent years campaigning against high-rise development at the site. “When residents bought their homes here, they did so expecting a mix of low and medium density housing in the area, not thousands of units in buildings up to 27 storeys,” he said. Local resident Olde Lorenzen pictured at the Little Bay site. Louise Kennerley Lorenzen said residents wanted assurances that the state government’s planning pathway would not pave the way for further increases in density. “It’s a step in the right direction, but our concern is that Meriton is using a state-significant pathway and we’ll be looking for clear assurances that what begins as 505 homes doesn’t become the start of a push for even greater density.

Advertisement

“We’re not anti-development, we just want sustainable development for the site, which is in a sensitive coastal environment.” The prolonged vacancy of the site had also created problems for nearby residents, he said, due to issues including trespassing and antisocial behaviour. Little Bay Cove has footpaths, roads – but no homes. Sam Mooy “Even though it’s fenced off, it’s regularly accessed by cars, residents, and trespassers,” he said. “There’s a playground on there that is falling apart, the grass is overgrown, we’ve had issues with overflowing bins and vermin, and there’s crime and drug trading going on down there at night. It’s definitely not in a good state.”

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

NSW Votes ‘Not another suburb for luxury housing’: Liberals to unveil Long Bay housing plan Last week, the NSW Coalition opposition announced plans to close the Long Bay Correctional Complex, located about 200 metres north of Little Bay Cove, and redevelop the site for 12,000 homes if elected in March 2027. NSW Planning Minister Paul Scully dismissed the proposal as a “fantasy”, arguing it would cost taxpayers billions of dollars and create excessive density without adequate infrastructure. But he expressed support for the Little Bay development. “It is always good to see underutilised land being activated for new housing,” Scully said.

Advertisement

“From downsizers to families and young people, everyone should have the option to live in the community they choose.” He stressed, however, that the Housing Delivery Authority’s initial support did not guarantee approval, with the proposal still subject to merit-based assessment and community consultation. An artist impression of the housing plan for the site in 2019. Maroubra Labor MP Michael Daley, who has previously criticised Meriton’s larger development plans, also welcomed the reduction in building heights. “If Meriton’s current application broadly represents what was represented in the master plan, that would be a good result,” he said.

Advertisement

“What I don’t want to see is them gaining an approval and then coming back and asking for multiple changes.” Related Article NSW State Parliament ‘A fantasy’: Labor attacks Coalition’s 12,000-home Long Bay plan Randwick Mayor Clare Willington criticised the use of the Housing Delivery Authority pathway, warning it would remove local oversight and “take planning decisions out of the council’s hands.” “Little Bay is a community, not a blank canvas for developers. They deserve a guarantee that a modest proposal today won’t become something very different tomorrow,” she said. Long-time resident Peter Fagan said while lower building heights were a positive compromise, local infrastructure remained a pressing concern.

Advertisement

“Adding another 505 homes will put enormous pressure on roads that are already heavily congested, as well as schools and hospitals,” Fagan said. “Sydney needs more homes, but it also needs responsible planning. The two should go hand in hand.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important stories. Sign up for our Morning Edition newsletter.

title: Thousands turn out to be among the first to walk the new Walyalup Bridge
text:

NationalWARoads Thousands turn out to be among the first to walk the new Walyalup Bridge Hannah Murphy November 1, 2026 — 1:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The new Fremantle Traffic Bridge, named Walyalup Bridge, has officially opened. Pedestrians were first on the bridge for the festivities at 9am, with a local pipe band and dancers providing a show. Heather McNeill State government ministers, locals, business owners and media gathered on Saturday morning for the official unveiling of the new bridge, with Minister for Transport Rita Saffioti leading the ribbon cutting ceremony. Thousands of pedestrians gathered just after 9am to cross the bridge on Sunday morning, and it will be later opened to traffic. The old Fremantle Traffic Bridge was closed in February, with the new structure originally tipped to open in the first half of 2027. However, fast-tracked construction has enabled it to open early.

Advertisement

The new bridge has the same number of traffic lanes as the old bridge, but has a higher clearance for boats and wider pedestrian lanes. It also updates the old 86-year-old timber framing, with cantilevers and cable stay supports. The state government said construction had since provided more than 1400 jobs. However with the speed of construction came a hefty price tag, with the original cost of the new bridge jumping from $430 million to $596 million in this year’s state budget. Saffioti said at the opening on Sunday the project had been worth the effort.

Advertisement

“Opening it ahead of schedule is an incredible achievement for everyone involved, and I congratulate the entire project team for their innovation and commitment to delivering it as quickly as possible,” she said. “Thank you to the local families, residents, businesses, schools and freight operators who have all played their part to keep the road network moving while we built this spectacular new bridge.” Throughout the bridge’s construction, some Fremantle businesses said they had felt the sting of the closures. Cellarbrations on Canning Highway closed after 17 years in business due to losing customers during the building, while other businesses reported a significant decline in profits and foot traffic due to roadworks. Member for Fremantle Simone McGurk also thanked her constituents for their patience, while Member for Bicton Lisa O’Malley said she acknowledged it had been difficult for some businesses to get through the closure period.

Advertisement

“We know delivering landmark projects like this causes disruption and I can’t thank our community enough for the patience they’ve shown,” O’Malley said. Related Article Perth business ‘A lot of people are sad’: Freo businesses struggle over bridge woes “Residents and businesses in the Bicton electorate and beyond have played an important part in keeping traffic on our roads moving as smoothly possible. Now it’s time to celebrate this iconic new gateway to Fremantle that will be a part of our community’s story for generations to come.” Road access to and from Fremantle via Canning Highway will be re-opened now the bridge is up and running, and Beach Street will also be back open to traffic. Federal Member for Fremantle Josh Wilson said it was important the new bridge had elements of the port city’s long history incorporated into its design.

Advertisement

“Walyalup Bridge is a brilliant addition to our working port, with a name and design that shape Fremantle’s future by respecting its deep cultural and industrial heritage,” he said. “Our community helped shape this project and showed extraordinary patience through its construction, and it is especially fitting that we can open it early by walking across it together.” The bridge has some remaining works to be completed including a lighting test, but is now open to traffic. Some of the timber preserved from the original traffic bridge has been used to build a walkway under the new Walyalup structure, and designers have also kept the brass lantern orbs previously used to light the way for drivers in their same spot. They will still be lit every night.

In this Melbourne Cup Briefing, your wrap of racing news: Injured jockey Harry Coffey is sweating on last-minute medical clearance to take his place in Tuesday’s $10.2 million Melbourne Cup.

Joseph O’Brien’s racing manager Kevin Blake has called for emergencies to become part of the Melbourne Cup after stewards scratched Defiantly on Saturday due to concerns about his gait. Danny Russell

Injured jockey Harry Coffey is sweating on last-minute medical clearance to take his place in Tuesday’s $10.2 million Melbourne Cup. Coffey is booked to partner Ciaron Maher’s lightweight fancy Shockletz in the 3200-metre staying test, but is in a race against the clock to recover from a suspected broken collarbone. Harry Coffey (right) on his way back to the mounting yard. Getty Images Connections said Coffey underwent a small procedure on Sunday and was waiting on his doctor to determine whether his injuries were stable enough to ride.

Advertisement

The 31-year-old father of two took a heavy tumble in the second-last race on Derby Day, sending a shockwave across the Flemington crowd. Racegoers feared for his safety as images on the big screen showed Coffey being catapulted into the air after his mount Pondalowie clipped heels and fell. “He has not been ruled in, he has not been ruled out,” Coffey’s manager Dean Hawkes said of the Cup ride on Sunday. The 2024 Caulfield Cup-winning hoop’s ability to cope with pain was evident after Saturday’s mid-race fall. He pulled himself to his feet and walked back to the mounting yard, cradling his arm, before taking part in a stewards’ inquiry. He was then taken to hospital.

Advertisement

Pondalowie was captured by a clerk of the course in the Flemington straight after the scary incident. The six-year-old mare was cleared of injury by vets. The fall happened at the 500m mark and had officials on high alert, following a horse death during the Caulfield Cup earlier this month. After speaking to Coffey, stewards released a report clearing all riders of any blame. “It was established that when the tempo quickened, Pondalowie, despite the efforts of Coffey, shifted in slightly when laying in, resulting in Pondalowie clipping the heels of Cilacap and falling,” stewards said. Maher and Shockletz’s connections will be anxiously awaiting Coffey’s call in case they need to find a replacement rider for the Cup third favourite.

Advertisement

“We’ll give Harry every opportunity and if he can’t do it we’ll find someone else,” Maher said at the Melbourne Cup barrier draw. “It’s a legitimate chance, so anybody would be disappointed if they were riding that horse and they weren’t able to [through injury].” Lightweight jockey Michael Dee has put his hand up for the Shockletz gig if Coffey is ruled out. He gave up his ride on mare Strictly Business, which will be ridden by Dean Yendall. ‘I don’t feel that’s good enough’: International crack at Melbourne Cup technology

Advertisement

Peter Ryan

Joseph O’Brien’s racing manager Kevin Blake has called for emergencies to become part of the Melbourne Cup after stewards scratched Defiantly on Saturday due to concerns about his gait. The stewards had to make the decision three days out from the race due to the need to lock in the field of 24 at 4.30pm on Saturday, despite the fact the horse may have made the necessary improvement in the remaining two days to take his place. Kevin Blake (left) suggested the technology used for the Melbourne Cup needed to be updated. Getty Images Emergencies are considered impossible because betting technology can’t handle late inclusions to a field of 24. It means if there are late scratchings between 4.30pm Saturday and the race start, fewer runners will race rather than the next qualified horses in the order of entry being granted a start.

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

Melbourne Cup Racing dodges another nightmare after mid-race fall; Derby Day trainer charged by stewards “We know it’s rigorous, we know it’s tough, and so we’re not going to cry about [the decision]. We’re all big boys and girls, but probably the main takeaway from it is they probably need to sort out their emergency situation,” Blake said. “I’m a guest here so I don’t want to be telling people what to do, but for the reason to be that the technology can’t cope with more than 24 runners in 2026 … I don’t feel that’s good enough.” Defiantly’s withdrawal gives stablemate Kizlyar a start, meaning the O’Brien stable still has five runners – but it robs the race of a natural leader, with the four-year-old gelding a noted frontrunner. Blake said the jockey Dylan Browne McMonagle, who had been booked to ride Defiantly, would now jump on Sons And Lovers, who was the best drawn of their five starters with barrier three.

Advertisement

He said local jockeys James McDonald and Craig Williams would need to weave some magic to their mounts Trustyourinstinct and James J Braddock in a good spot after they drew barriers 18 and 24 respectively. Related Melbourne Cup Pick your winners with our 2026 Melbourne Cup sweep McDonald is the in-form jockey after an exhilarating Derby Day where he won four races including the Derby and Trustyourinstinct is sure to win support due to his presence in the saddle. “James is going to have to work his magic to get in and get cover [and] get him racing efficiently, but he is a very classy horse unexposed to the trip,” Blake said. “[He] looks to have a leading chance in the book, so you just hope he gets a kind spin from the draw.”

Advertisement

Last year’s runner-up Goodie Two Shoes is said to be in better form than last season and is expected to carry big bets from his owner J.P. McManus. Blake also talked up Kizlyar’s chances despite his disappointing run in the Moonee Valley Cup, which became a sit and sprint at the finish. Defiantly may run in the Queen Elizabeth Stakes on Saturday as a consolation, with O’Brien due to fly in from the Breeders’ Cup, which is raced in the US, on Monday. Meanwhile at Werribee, Ethan Brown was pleased with Point of Law’s work on Sunday when he visited the horse he rode to victory in the Geelong Cup. Ryan to front stewards inquiry Danny Russell

Trainer Nick Ryan is expected to front a Racing Victoria stewards inquiry on Monday on a charge of possessing syringes containing a synthetic EPO.

Advertisement

Stewards raided Ryan’s Flemington stables on Derby Day morning and allegedly found syringes in the glove box of his car containing Darbepoetin Alfa – a man-made stimulating agent that mimics a natural hormone. Darbepoetin Alfa is listed as a prohibited substance under the rules of racing. As a result, Ryan’s two runners on Derby Day – Doubt Time and Anglais – were scratched. Stewards will seek further evidence from the former jockey at Monday’s hearing after he reserved his plea on Saturday. The hearing will be closed. Stewards have the power to suspend Ryan until the charge against him is heard if they believe his case prejudices the “image, interests, integrity or welfare of racing”. They will also decide on Monday whether Ryan can run last-start winner Terrortorian in the second race at Flemington on Melbourne Cup Day.

title: Inside the scramble to contain the largest crypto heist in history
text:

BusinessMarketsCryptocurrencies Inside the scramble to contain the largest crypto heist in history Ben Weiss , Muyao Shen and Olga Kharif November 1, 2026 — 12:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The biggest crypto hack in history began with a rehearsal. As trading hummed along on Binance, hackers were quietly running sequences of code on accounts they controlled on the Ethereum blockchain — just a couple of dollars or so at a time. According to cybersecurity analysts, they were testing a program designed to seize control of accounts owned by the world’s largest crypto exchange and smuggle their contents elsewhere. Just after 4pm (New York time) on Thursday, they attacked. Binance, the largest crypto exchange in the world, was hit by a massive hack late last week. Getty Images In short order, the infiltrators drained more than $US6 billion ($8.9 billion) from wallets across at least four different blockchains, setting off a worldwide effort to contain the damage.

Advertisement

From New York to Abu Dhabi and Kyiv, security researchers and Binance executives scrambled to trace the stolen money, freeze accounts and understand how the attackers had breached the exchange and pulled off a heist that has shaken confidence in the crypto industry as it tries to earn greater acceptance in finance’s mainstream. “It’s the largest bank robbery in human history,” said Ari Redbord, global head of policy and government affairs at TRM Labs, a blockchain analytics firm. Redbord’s firm was one of several that mobilised after the attack started. “I literally haven’t slept and I haven’t stopped.” Related Article Cryptocurrencies ‘Biggest hack in history’: Crypto giant freezes assets after $8.9b heist As Binance publicly said it could easily reimburse any losses from the hack on Friday, employees were privately expressing doubts to one another that they’d be paid bonuses this year, according to people familiar with the matter.

Advertisement

The crypto industry is no stranger to malevolent actors. Only a month ago, cryptocurrency exchange Bitget was subject to a cyberattack that drained $US388 million. In February 2025, hackers stole nearly $US1.5 billion from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit. But the scale of this week’s attack shocked even industry veterans. Just as the exploit was unleashed, Taylor Monahan, who’s based in Los Angeles as a researcher at the non-profit security firm, SEAL, was on a group chat with other crypto investigators when someone at blockchain security firm zeroShadow sent a message about strange transactions at Binance. “I’m going to remain optimistic that everything’s fine,” Monahan told herself. But she knew that if things weren’t OK, they were very bad. “It’s like a hack — like, a really big one.” By 4.38pm, Monahan suspected the worst and contacted Tether, the firm that issues the USDT dollar-backed stablecoin. “In our souls, we knew it was a hack,” she said. Tether responded immediately but didn’t acknowledge that there was an infiltration. Less than 30 minutes later, the firm began the process of freezing the transactions on its blockchain, as did Circle, issuer of the USDC stablecoin. Scrolling X

Advertisement

Yi He, Binance’s co-founder and co-chief executive officer, was at home in Abu Dhabi when she first noticed something wrong. The executive had logged off work and was scrolling through X before going to bed about 12.30am in Abu Dhabi (4.30pm in New York). Posts on the social media site alerted her to trouble. Alarmed, she logged back on and saw that Binance’s security and wallet teams – which are empowered to act on hacks without executive sign off – were already at work, trying to stop more losses. Within minutes, the company created a war room that swelled to about 100 people around the world. Yi and hundreds of Binance employees would stay up through the night, co-ordinating efforts within the company and with other crypto firms and law-enforcement agencies including the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the US Secret Service. Binance’s co-founder and co-chief executive, Yi He, was alerted to the trouble by posts on X. Natalie Naccache At 5.15pm (New York time), Binance publicly acknowledged it was aware of a “potential security issue” and that it was investigating the rumoured breach.

Advertisement

At 5.18pm, Circle chief executive Jeremy Allaire announced the stablecoin company had frozen more than $US800 million associated with a “potential exploit involving Binance”. Seven minutes later, Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino announced that his firm had frozen more than $US1.5 billion “related to a potential Binance exchange hack”. Related Article Cryptocurrencies Inside a billionaire’s paradise with crypto’s most powerful ex-convict Soon, crypto companies of every stripe started flooding social media to promise onlookers that they were safe. Binance competitors, including Kraken, Coinbase and Bybit, proclaimed they were unharmed. Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs, Chainalysis and Elliptic have all said North Korea is behind the heist. They observed funds stolen from Binance commingle with crypto seized in the Bitget hack, which researchers had already attributed to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. At the weekend, the FBI also blamed North Korea for the hack.

Advertisement

Chainalysis labelled the hack as “the largest in the history of crypto, and one of the single-largest financial crimes of all time”. Still, even as the heist became more widely publicised, hackers continued to drain funds from Binance. The code attackers used gave them access to blockchain accounts owned by Binance and let the hackers empty them, all while exchange funds kept replenishing the accounts. Estimates of the amount stolen crept higher, eventually reaching $US6.3 billion. Mainstream crypto The attack comes at an inopportune time for an industry that is getting unprecedented support from the US government. The Trump administration has been pushing for mainstream adoption of cryptocurrencies and blockchain technology, including through its regulators. In September, the Securities and Exchange Commission approved a rule that allows for public company stocks to trade on blockchains. The Binance hack could undermine those efforts, experts fear. Odysseas Lamtzidis, founder of blockchain security company Phylax Systems, was on a plane travelling to Miami from New York when he saw a Telegram chat discussing the attack. “It was very scary. I remember breathing heavy because it was huge amounts of capital moving around, and people on the plane were asking if I was OK,” he said.

Advertisement

‘It’s still a Wild West.’ Odysseas Lamtzidis, founder of Phylax Systems, He watched as the attackers moved from one wallet to the next, and kept posting on X to alert users. “I think this is very scary for organisations and adoption of crypto because these types of events should be impossible to happen, not improbable,” he said. “It’s still a Wild West.” Binance co-chief executive Richard Teng. Dominic Lorrimer Yi and her co-chief executive, Richard Teng, on Friday confronted the potential reputational damage the attack could do. In a video posted on X, Yi promised Binance would continue to work with law enforcement to find the attackers. The company has vowed to reimburse any users who lost funds in the hack.

Advertisement

“We won’t let the hackers take away the momentum this industry deserves,” she said in her video post, speaking in Mandarin. “Of course, there are areas where we could have done better. We should have invested more in security earlier, and set stricter standards. Going forward, we won’t hold back, whether it’s investing in security or fighting hackers.” On Saturday, the company said it had restored 90 per cent of the tokens which hackers had stolen, pledging to reinstate customers’ ability to withdraw funds the following day. Related Article Opinion

Cryptocurrencies Trump has made billions from crypto. It just backfired on him Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Asked about employees’ bonus concerns, a spokesperson said Binance didn’t expect any impact there either. In the midst of the turmoil, some traders found opportunity.

Advertisement

Morten Christensen, a cryptocurrency trader who also runs AirdropAlert.com, a site that tracks cryptocurrency giveaways, made tens of thousands of dollars on Thursday. He was in Mexico, on a Discord call with six friends, brainstorming strategies to take advantage of the hack. They had decided to short cryptocurrencies, which were starting to drop in value when his wife walked into his office. He sent her back out. “Binance got hacked, babe,” he said. “Need to lock in.” With assistance from Ryan Weeks and Teresa Xie Bloomberg The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. St George Illawarra and Cronulla target Jack Bostock will meet with his management this week to weigh up his options, and he has not ruled out extending his stay at the Dolphins. One of 11 Kangaroos now free to accept offers from rival clubs, Bostock is doing everything possible to drive up his price following another three tries for Australia in their 66-6 thrashing of the Cook Islands on Saturday night. Loading Arguably the best winger in the game but someone who wants to play centre in the NRL, Bostock has been heavily linked with the Dragons, along with the Sharks and even Parramatta, who are also chasing fellow Kangaroo Bradman Best. Depending on what happens to Dolphins centre and primary Roosters target Herbie Farnworth, the Illawarra junior could even pop up on the radar of the NRL premiers.

Advertisement

When asked about relocating back home, Bostock said: “It’s definitely not 100 per cent set in stone [that] I’m coming to Sydney. I’m not sure where that’s come from. “I spoke to the Dolphins a couple of weeks ago and said I wanted to see my options and what I could do. Jack Bostock will meet with his management this week. Getty Images “It’s not set in stone I’m leaving the Dolphins. It’s a matter of going through the process. It’s hard to do while you’re in here because the task at hand is winning the World Cup. “Once I can sort out a time with my manager, we’ll sit down during the week, or have a phone call, and start figuring out what we’re going to do.

Advertisement

“We can see how many players are coming off on November 1. It’s been a running joke in camp about who is going where and what’s going to happen.” Kangaroos fullback Reece Walsh urged Bostock to come to the Broncos, especially now the club has signed Peter O’Sullivan, the recruitment chief who brought Bostock to the Dolphins. Loading Bostock, who also made his NSW Origin debut this year, is in line to earn as much as $900,000 a season. “What is he, 23?,” Walsh asked.

Advertisement

“He’s hardworking, can play many positions, and you can see he’s still growing into his body. “He’s an awesome talent who works really hard. He knows when to flick the switch, work hard at training, but he’s also a character off the field and has a laugh. Related Article NRL 2026 ‘It makes sense to us’: Meninga wants to reunite Burton and Sexton at the Bears “It’s interesting to see all the [contract] yarns getting thrown around; obviously there have been jokes and a bit of chat here and there, but I don’t think it’s hindered anyone’s training or connection or their presence in [Kangaroos] camp.” Some of the game’s biggest names are officially ready to open negotiations for 2028, none more so than Nathan Cleary. The Penrith playmaker, however, is expected to extend his stay with the club.

Advertisement

Sam Walker’s contract talks broke down with the Sydney Roosters, and he has been linked to Canterbury, especially if Matt Burton takes up a lucrative offer with Perth, whose coach Mal Meninga is eager to work with the five-eighth. Hudson Young is tipped to tour the PNG Chiefs’ Port Moresby base in the coming weeks now that his own extension offer with Canberra was officially spiked, while Harry Grant and Cameron Munster are prepared to test their worth before deciding whether they recommit to the Melbourne Storm. Meanwhile, Bostock’s hat-trick means he still trails Tom Trbojevic by one try in this tournament, as the Manly star also bagged another treble in Townsville. “He’s got me, hasn’t he? It would be silly to have a wager now; we haven’t had a bet, but he can score all of them, as long as we’re winning,” Bostock said. title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
